paragraphs.text: One fine June morning, Miss Polly Harrington hurried into her kitchen. Nancy, who was busy washing dishes, looked up in surprise. Although Nancy had worked for Miss Polly for only two months, she'd never seen her employer hurry.
"Nancy," Miss Polly said.
"Yes, ma'am," Nancy answered cheerfully as she continued drying a pitcher.
"When I'm speaking, you should stop working and listen," Miss Polly said in a stern voice.
Nancy set the pitcher on the counter and almost tipped it over. "Yes, ma'am, I will. I only kept working because you said to hurry with the dishes this morning."
Miss Polly frowned. "I didn't ask for explanations. I asked for your attention."
"Yes, ma'am." Nancy struggled not to sigh.

This was Nancy's first job, and she wondered if there was any way to please Miss Polly. Nancy had needed to find work when her father died suddenly. Her sick mother was left with Nancy, who was 16, and 3 younger children.

Before Nancy was hired, she only knew Miss Polly as one of the wealthiest residents of Beldingsville, Vermont. Now Nancy knew her as a demanding woman who frowned if silverware clattered to the floor or doors banged. Miss Polly never smiled, even when forks and doors were silent. And she never gave Nancy a word of praise.
"I want you to clean up the little room in the attic," Miss Polly said. "After you remove the trunks and boxes, sweep the floor. Then set up the cot."
"And where should I put the things I remove?"
"In the front attic." Miss Polly paused for a moment. "I suppose I should tell you that my niece, Miss Pollyanna Whittier, is coming to live with me. She's 11 years old, and that will be her room."
Nancy's face broke into a wide grin. "A little girl living here? Oh, that'll be nice!"
"Nice? That isn't exactly the word I'd use." Miss Polly sniffed. "However, I intend to make the best of the situation. I'm a good woman, and I know my duty."
Nancy blushed. "Of course, ma'am. I wasn't saying that you weren't good. I mean . . . I was only thinking that . . . well . . . a child might brighten things up for you."
"I don't see any need for that." Miss Polly abruptly turned to leave the kitchen. "Make sure you clean the corners of the room," she called over her shoulder.
"Yes, ma'am." Nancy sighed and went back to drying dishes.
A short time later, Miss Polly sat in her room, rereading a letter. When the letter had arrived from out West, it contained an unpleasant surprise.
Dear Miss Harrington,

I regret to inform you that the Reverend John Whittier has died, making his daughter, Pollyanna, an orphan. A poor minister, he left nothing except a few books. I know that Reverend Whittier was your late sister's husband. Although your families didn't get along, he thought you might want to bring up Pollyanna, for your sister's sake.

A local couple is traveling to Boston this week, so they can accompany Pollyanna for most of the journey. In Boston, they'll put Pollyanna on a train to Beldingsville. I'll let you know what train she is on.
I hope to hear from you soon.
Sincerely,
Jeremiah White

Miss Polly shook her head as she remembered her sister Jennie, Pollyanna's mother. When Jennie was twenty, she'd married Whittier against the wishes of her parents. They'd wanted her to marry a wealthy, older man, but she'd chosen the minister and moved far away. Miss Polly was 15 when her oldest sister married. For a while Jennie wrote to her family, although they never replied.
All Jennie's babies died except Pollyanna. Jennie named the baby for her two sisters, Polly and Anna. A few years later, Whittier wrote to say Jennie had died.

Miss Polly was forty now and alone in the world. Her parents and two sisters had all died. Some people pitied her lonely life and urged her to have a friend live with her. But Miss Polly welcomed neither their sympathy nor their advice. She wasn't lonely; she liked being by herself and preferred quiet.
Miss Polly stood up and put away the letter. "I'll do my duty and take in Jennie's daughter. But Pollyanna —what a ridiculous name!"
Nancy put all her energy into scrubbing and sweeping the little attic room. Remembering Miss Polly's instructions, she made sure the corners were especially clean.
"I wish I could clean out the corners of Miss Polly's heart," Nancy said as she swept up a cloud of dust.
Nancy was afraid of Miss Polly, but she also had plenty of opinions about her employer.

"The idea of sticking that poor child way up here in this hot, tiny room!" Nancy stopped to wipe some sweat from her face. "In summer it's uncomfortable, and in winter there won't be any fireplace to warm her. With all the nice rooms in this house, Miss Polly picked this one? Unbelievable!"
For a while Nancy worked in silence. Then she looked around the room in disgust. There were no pictures or colorful curtains; there was nothing to make the space bright or cheerful.
"Well, my part's done." Nancy wrung out a wet rag until her fingers ached. "There's no dirt here—or anything else. What a terrible place to put a homesick, lonely child!"
Nancy left the room and slammed the door. "Oops!" Nancy bit her lip in fear. Then she stood up tall and said, "I don't care! I hope Miss Polly heard that and was annoyed!"

Nancy went into the backyard, where Tom, the gardener, was pulling weeds. She looked quickly over her shoulder to be sure Miss Polly wasn't watching. "Tom, did you know a child is coming to live here?"
"Coming to live with Miss Polly?" The old man straightened up with difficulty. "You must be joking."
"Miss Polly told me herself. It's her niece, Pollyanna, and she's an 11-year-old orphan."
Tom smiled. "That must be Miss Jennie's girl. I can't believe these old eyes will actually get to see her."
"Who's Miss Jennie?" Nancy asked.
"She was Miss Polly's sister, and she was wonderful," Tom said. "Such a kind person. Miss Jennie left here to marry a minister a long time ago. Last we heard she'd died."
"Well, Miss Polly is making Pollyanna sleep in the attic." Nancy glanced over her shoulder again to be sure Miss Polly wasn’t nearby. "Miss Polly should be ashamed of herself!"
Tom went back to pulling weeds but started chuckling.
"What's so funny?" Nancy asked, squatting next to him.
"I wonder what Miss Polly will do with a child in the house."
"Humph! I wonder what a child will do with Miss Polly in the house."
Now Tom was laughing heartily. "It's obvious you're not fond of Miss Polly."
"As if anybody could be fond of her!" Nancy yanked out a weed and tossed it into Tom's wheelbarrow.
Tom raised his eyebrows. "I guess you don't know about Miss Polly's broken engagement."
"Broken engagement? Her ?"
Tom nodded. "The fellow still lives right here in town."
"Who is it?" Nancy looked at him eagerly.
Tom put a hand on his aching back and stood up. "No, no, I can't tell you. It's not right that I reveal Miss Polly's secret."
"It just doesn't seem possible."
"Think of it like a mystery in one of those books you're always reading," Tom teased her.
Nancy shook her head. "I still don't believe that anyone could be in love with Miss Polly."
"Years ago Miss Polly was quite pretty, and she would be now . . ." Tom hesitated. "If she let herself."
"Pretty? Miss Polly?"
"Yes, she didn't always pull her hair back so tight. She used to wear flowers on her bonnets and lace trim on her dresses. If she did all that again, you'd see she's not so old."
"Well, she does a good imitation of a cranky old person. There's no pleasing her now."
"That's certainly true. It all started with that argument with her sweetheart."
"She shouldn't take it out on us," Nancy said. "If my family didn't need the money, I'd quit. One day I'll get so mad that I'll say something I shouldn't, and she'll fire me."
"Nancy!" a sharp voice called from a window.
Nancy's eyes widened in fear, and she dashed for the house. "Yes, ma'am! I'm coming, ma'am!"

The afternoon before Pollyanna's arrival, Miss Polly inspected the attic room. A fly buzzed at one of the closed windows, trying to escape. Miss Polly killed the fly, opened the window, and swept the fly outside. Then she went downstairs and stood at the kitchen door.
"Nancy," Miss Polly said. "I found a fly in Miss Pollyanna's room. Until the new screens come, keep the windows closed."
Nancy stopped ironing. "Yes, ma'am."

"My niece will arrive tomorrow afternoon at four o'clock," Miss Polly went on. "Tom will drive you to the station to meet her. The telegram said, 'blond hair, red gingham dress, straw hat.' That's all I know, but that's enough information for you to find her."
"Yes, ma'am," Nancy said again. "But shouldn't you—"
"No, I don't need to go." Miss Polly walked away.
Nancy picked up her iron. "Blond hair, red gingham dress, straw hat. I'd be ashamed to admit that's all I know about my only niece."

The next afternoon Tom drove Nancy to the station. As the train whistle sounded, Nancy was suddenly nervous. But she soon spotted a girl with two blond braids in a red gingham dress. Beneath a straw hat, an eager freckled face looked all around.
Nancy approached the child. "Are you Miss Pollyanna?"
"Yes!" The next moment Pollyanna was hugging Nancy tightly. "I'm so glad, glad, glad to see you! Of course I'm Pollyanna, and I hoped you'd come to meet me."
"You did?" Nancy couldn't understand how Pollyanna knew she'd be at the station.
"I've been wondering what you looked like." Pollyanna danced around Nancy. "I'm glad you look just like you do."
Nancy didn't know how to reply. She was relieved when Tom walked over and offered to find Pollyanna's trunk.

"It's a brand-new trunk," Pollyanna explained as Nancy guided her toward the wagon. "The Ladies' Aid—the women's group at Father's church—was saving money for a new church carpet. But the ladies bought me a trunk instead. Anyway, the Ladies' Aiders—do you have Ladies' Aiders at your church? Father said many churches do. They helped Father bring me up after Mother died."

Pollyanna kept up a stream of comments and questions. By the time Tom returned with the trunk, Nancy was dazed and breathless. But Pollyanna was still full of energy. She climbed up and sat between them.

"This is lovely!" Pollyanna said as they started on their way. "Is it far to your house? I hope it is because I love to ride. But if it isn't, I'll be glad to get there soon. What a pretty town! I knew this town would be pretty. Father told me he remembered—"
Pollyanna stopped, and Nancy noticed her eyes filling with tears. But in a moment, the little girl hurried on.

"I suppose you wonder why I'm wearing red instead of black for mourning. There wasn't anything black in the donation box at church. Do you have donation boxes here? They're full of clothes and things that people don't want anymore. But they think poor people will want them."
"I'm sure your dress will be fine," Nancy said.
"It would be harder to be glad in black."
"Glad?" Nancy said in surprise.

"Yes, glad that Father has gone to heaven to be with Mother and their babies. He said I must be glad, which was awfully hard when I just had the Ladies' Aid. But now I've got you, Aunt Polly, and I'm so glad!"
Nancy's eyes widened as she realized Pollyanna's mistake. "I'm not your aunt Polly. I'm only Nancy, a girl who works for her!"
"Oh," Pollyanna said anxiously. "But there is an Aunt Polly, right?"
Tom chuckled. "There sure is."
Pollyanna relaxed. "Then I'm glad I can look forward to meeting her. Is Aunt Polly rich, Nancy?"
"Yes, miss."

"I hope she has carpets and pictures in every room. I love pictures, but we didn't have any. Father found one in the donation box. It was so nice that he sold it to buy me shoes. What a beautiful house!" Pollyanna exclaimed as they came up the drive.
Nancy thought about the plain attic room and silently vowed to stay at Miss Polly's house forever. "This poor child needs someone to love her!"
When Pollyanna arrived, Miss Polly was reading in her sitting room. She didn't bother to stand up but extended a hand for Pollyanna to shake.
"How do you do, Pollyanna? I—"
Pollyanna raced across the room and threw her arms around her startled relative.
"Aunt Polly! I'm so glad you're letting me live with you!" Pollyanna sobbed with relief, burying her face in Aunt Polly's lap.
"I'm sure that's true." Aunt Polly tried to loosen Pollyanna's grip around her waist. "Please be good enough to stand up straight. I don't even know what you look like."
Pollyanna stood up at once. "I should explain why I'm wearing red instead of black. I told Nancy how Father said—"
"Never mind what he said," Aunt Polly interrupted. "You've brought a trunk, I assume?"
"Yes, indeed. I don't have many things of my own. But the Ladies' Aiders thought I should bring Father's books and—"
"Pollyanna!" Aunt Polly interrupted again. "There's something we should get straight right away. I don't want to hear anything about your father."
Pollyanna looked startled. "You mean . . . nothing at all?"
"It's time to go upstairs to your room," Aunt Polly said, changing the subject.
Silently, Pollyanna followed her aunt from the sitting room. Her eyes were filled with tears, but she bravely held her chin high. She thought Aunt Polly was probably being kind.
"I'm glad Aunt Polly doesn't want to talk about Father," Pollyanna thought. "Maybe if I don't talk about him, I won't miss him so much."

They were in an upstairs hallway now, and Pollyanna eagerly admired the thick rugs and pictures in gold frames. Open doors offered glimpses into beautifully furnished bedrooms with lace curtains at the windows. Pollyanna couldn't wait to see which bedroom was hers.
"Oh, Aunt Polly, you have so many pretty things. You must be glad you're rich!" Pollyanna exclaimed.
"Pollyanna!" Aunt Polly scolded. "We do not talk about money in this family!"

Aunt Polly's instinct had been to put her niece as far away from herself as possible. She knew children were careless, so the attic was perfect. It contained nothing valuable that Pollyanna could ruin. Now that Aunt Polly had met Pollyanna, she'd seen that this girl was very interested in money and possessions. Her instinct had been right!
Aunt Polly opened a door, and they went upstairs into the dim, hot attic. Pollyanna couldn't imagine why Aunt Polly was taking her someplace where it was hard to breathe.
"Here's your room," Aunt Polly said, opening a door. "I see Tom has brought up your trunk. Do you have the key?"
Pollyanna nodded. Her eyes were wide with fright.
"When I ask a question, Pollyanna, I'd like you to speak."
"Yes, Aunt Polly."
"Thank you, that's better." Aunt Polly glanced at the water pitcher, which Nancy had filled. "I believe you have everything you need. I'll send Nancy to help you unpack. Supper is at six o'clock."
Aunt Polly abruptly went downstairs, leaving Pollyanna alone. When Nancy came up a few minutes later, she found Pollyanna sobbing.
"Oh, you poor lamb!" Nancy dropped to the floor and hugged Pollyanna. "Let's hang up your dresses."
"I don't have many."
"Then it'll be a quick job," Nancy said.
Pollyanna suddenly smiled. "Well, I can be glad about that!"
Nancy didn't know how to respond. She quickly unpacked Pollyanna's patched underwear and out-of-style dresses. Nancy suspected they'd all come from the donation box.

"This will be a nice room," Pollyanna said, looking out a window. "Don't you think? I'm glad there isn't a mirror because now I can't see my freckles. And the view from this window is better than any picture. I'm so glad Aunt Polly let me have this room!"
To Pollyanna's surprise, Nancy stifled a sob and ran downstairs.
Left alone, Pollyanna opened the window and let in the cool, fresh air along with some flies. She smiled mischievously as she studied the tree outside. "I bet I could climb down this tree!"

An hour later the hall clock struck six, and Nancy rang the bell for supper. Five minutes passed, and there was no sign of Pollyanna. Aunt Polly stepped into the hall and listened intently. For a moment she waited, tapping her foot impatiently. Then she swept into the dining room.
Aunt Polly was sitting alone in the dining room when Nancy brought in supper.
"My niece will have to suffer the consequences for being late," Aunt Polly said. "When Pollyanna comes downstairs, she may have bread and milk in the kitchen."
"Yes, ma'am." Nancy made a face, but fortunately Aunt Polly didn't catch her.
Right after supper Nancy crept up the back stairs to the attic.
"The poor lamb probably cried herself to sleep," Nancy said. She softly opened Pollyanna's door. The next moment she gave a frightened cry. "Pollyanna? Where are you?"
Nancy looked in the closet, under the bed, and even in the trunk. Then she flew downstairs and out to the garden.
"Tom! Pollyanna is missing!"
"What?" Tom stopped tying some roses to a trellis. He scanned the horizon and pointed to a small figure silhouetted against the evening sky. "There she is—on top of that hill!"
"Oh no! Miss Polly will see her!" Nancy said. "I don't want her to get a scolding. She's already in trouble for missing supper."
By the time Nancy reached Pollyanna, the older girl was out of breath. "Pollyanna, you gave me a scare," Nancy said, panting. "I didn't know where you were!"
"You don't need to worry about me," Pollyanna said as they came down the hill hand in hand. "Father and the Ladies' Aiders used to worry when I wandered off. Then they realized I always came back."
"How did you leave your room without anyone seeing you?" Nancy asked.
"I climbed down the tree outside my window."
"Oh my goodness!" Nancy exclaimed. "I'd like to know what your aunt would say about that."
Pollyanna patted Nancy's arm. "Then I'll tell Aunt Polly, so you can find out!"
Nancy's eyes widened in alarm. "No, no! Don't do that!"
Pollyanna looked surprised but she nodded.
"You must be hungry," Nancy said quickly. "But Miss Polly said you must eat bread and milk in the kitchen because you were late for supper."
"I like bread and milk," Pollyanna said happily as they entered the kitchen. "And I won't have any trouble being glad about eating with you."
Nancy remembered Pollyanna's brave attempt to like her attic room. "You don't have any trouble being glad about most things."
Pollyanna laughed softly. "That's the whole point of the game."
"The game?" Nancy gave Pollyanna a puzzled look as she set bread and milk on the table.

"Yes, the Glad Game! Father and I played it all the time." Pollyanna took a big drink of milk. "It all started when I wanted a doll. Every week Father looked in the donation box at church. There were all kinds of toys and clothes and other things in there, but no doll. Finally he brought home a pair of crutches that were just my size."
"Crutches?" Nancy said.

"Yes!" Pollyanna clapped her hands with glee. "It wasn't a doll, but Father said, 'Just be glad you don't need crutches!' And so we began playing a game to find things to be glad about. Sometimes it's difficult to think of something. But that makes the game even more fun!"
Nancy was still skeptical.
"It's going to be harder to play the game without Father," Pollyanna admitted. "But maybe Aunt Polly will play it with me."
"I don't think so!" Nancy blurted out. Noticing the disappointment on Pollyanna's face, she quickly made a promise. "But I'll do my best to play it with you."
That satisfied Pollyanna, who finished up her bread and milk. Then she went into the sitting room, where Aunt Polly was reading.
"It's time for bed," Aunt Polly said. "I regret having to punish you on your first day here."

"I was glad you did, Aunt Polly. I like bread and milk, and Nancy too. So don't feel bad about that." Pollyanna gave her aunt an affectionate hug. "I've had a wonderful time so far. I know I'm going to love living with you. Good night!"
"What an unusual child!" Aunt Polly said to herself as Pollyanna ran from the room.
But a few minutes later, Pollyanna was sobbing herself to sleep. "Oh, Father!" she said softly. "Even you would have trouble being glad about sleeping way up here by yourself."
When Pollyanna awoke the next morning, it was a beautiful day. Through an open window, she spotted Aunt Polly and Tom in the garden. Pollyanna ran outside and threw her arms around her aunt.
"Aunt Polly! Aunt Polly! Today I'm glad just to be alive!"
"Is this how you usually say good morning?" Aunt Polly scolded, releasing herself from Pollyanna's grip.
"Only to people I love!" Pollyanna danced around Aunt Polly, who tried to frown but failed.
"You may finish trimming those roses," Aunt Polly said to Tom. Then she hurried into the house.
"You're so like your mother, little miss," said Tom, picking up his clippers. "I knew her when she was your age."
Pollyanna gasped. "You did? Oh, please, tell me all about her!"
Tom had barely begun to speak when a bell sounded from the house. The next minute Nancy flew out the back door.
"Hurry up!" Nancy pulled Pollyanna toward the house. "That bell means it's time to eat. If you don't come quickly, it'll be hard to find anything to be glad about."
At the breakfast table, Aunt Polly and Pollyanna ate in silence. As Nancy brought in more muffins, Aunt Polly noticed two flies. "Nancy, where did those flies come from?"
"I don't know, ma'am."
"They're probably my flies," Pollyanna said cheerfully. "A whole bunch of them were having a wonderful time in my room this morning."
Struggling not to laugh, Nancy left the room with the muffins.
"Nancy!" Aunt Polly called.
Nancy returned with a serious look on her face and the muffins.
"You may put down the muffins and close the windows in Miss Pollyanna's room," Aunt Polly said. "Pollyanna, keep those windows closed until we have screens. Flies spread all kinds of diseases."
After breakfast Aunt Polly handed Pollyanna a pamphlet on flies. Pollyanna's eyes lit up when she saw an enlarged illustration of a fly's head. "Thank you!" she exclaimed, skipping from the room.
Awhile later Aunt Polly went up to Pollyanna's room.
"Oh, Aunt Polly, I never read anything so interesting in my life!" Pollyanna said with great enthusiasm. "I'm so glad you gave me that article. I had no idea flies—"
"That's enough," said Aunt Polly, who'd meant the pamphlet as punishment for opening the windows. "I'd like to examine your clothes to see if they're suitable for living here with me."
With great reluctance, Pollyanna opened her closet. "I'm afraid you'll think they're awful. You see, they all came from the donation box at church. Did you ever get your clothes from a donation box?"

Seeing Aunt Polly's shocked face, Pollyanna quickly corrected herself. "Of course not. You're rich—though in this room it's easy for me to forget you're rich. It was hard to play the game with my clothes, but Fath—" Pollyanna stopped when she remembered Aunt Polly didn't want to hear about her father.
Aunt Polly abruptly started examining Pollyanna's clothes. "I assume you went to school?"
"Yes, and sometimes Fath—I mean, I was taught at home too."

Aunt Polly looked stern. "You'll start school in the fall, but in the meantime, you'll be on a strict schedule. Every day before breakfast, you'll tidy this room. At nine o'clock you'll read aloud to me for half an hour. On Wednesdays and Saturdays, you'll spend the rest of the morning in the kitchen with Nancy, learning to cook. On the other mornings, I'll teach you to sew. You'll spend your afternoons practicing the piano."
Pollyanna squirmed. "I don't really like playing the piano."
"I'm sure that's true, but you will take piano lessons here."
Pollyanna sighed deeply. "With all these activities, you haven't left me time to just live. You know, to climb hills and talk to Tom and explore the town."

Now it was Aunt Polly's turn to sigh. "I'm doing my duty by ensuring that you have proper care and instruction. You must do your duty too. Don't waste these opportunities and don't be ungrateful. There will be some time for play."
Aunt Polly was halfway down the stairs when Pollyanna called after her. "What did you think of my clothes?"
"We'll go shopping this afternoon. If I let you appear in public in those clothes, I wouldn't be doing my duty!"

That afternoon Aunt Polly and Pollyanna went shopping for clothes. After visiting five stores, Aunt Polly was exhausted. The clerks were amused by Pollyanna's conversation, and Pollyanna was delighted with the whole excursion.
Waiting for the last package to be wrapped, Pollyanna beamed with happiness.
"My clothes have always come from a church donation box," she explained to the clerk. "You can't imagine how lovely it is to have beautiful new clothes that fit!"

After supper Aunt Polly recovered from the shopping excursion by visiting a neighbor. Pollyanna sat in the backyard, chatting with Tom and Nancy. Tom told Pollyanna many wonderful things about her mother, while Nancy described the farm where her own family lived.
"If Miss Polly lets me, I'll take you there sometime," Nancy promised Pollyanna. "But now it's time for you to go to bed."
Pollyanna lit a candle and climbed the steps to the attic. Her little room was as hot as an oven. With a sigh, she looked at the two closed windows.
"I wish I could open them," she said, "but Aunt Polly said I must wait until the screens come."

After neatly folding her clothes, Pollyanna blew out the candle and got into bed. Unable to sleep, she tossed and turned for what seemed like hours. Finally, she slipped out of bed and felt her way through the darkness to her door.
"Maybe there's a window with screens in the main part of the attic," she said.
Pollyanna followed a beam of moonlight through the dark attic to a window.
"Oh dear, there's no screen here either. But wait a minute, what's that?"
Just below the window, Pollyanna spotted a wide, flat roof. "If only I could sleep out there!"

Behind her were the vast dark attic and her hot room. Ahead of her—through the window—were the moonlight and the cool night air. Suddenly Pollyanna noticed a row of long white bags hanging from nails.
"Nancy said those bags contain winter clothing, put away for the summer." Pollyanna studied the garment bags. "Maybe I could turn them into a bed."

Pollyanna selected a soft, thick bag for a mattress. She could fold up a thinner bag for a pillow. Gleefully, Pollyanna gathered up the bags and dropped them out the window. Then she carefully climbed outside, closing the window behind her.

Taking deep breaths of the refreshing air, Pollyanna danced with delight. She walked from one end of the roof to the other with no fear of falling off. Finally, with a sigh of contentment, she arranged the garment bags into a bed.
Settling down, she gazed at the star-filled sky. "I'm glad the screens haven't come yet," she said sleepily, "because now I can enjoy this lovely outdoor bed."
Meanwhile, downstairs in her room, Aunt Polly heard noises on the roof. She hurried into her bathrobe and slippers, and then phoned Tom.
"Come quick! Bring a lantern and a ladder!" Aunt Polly instructed Tom. "Somebody's on the roof. I'm going upstairs to make sure the attic window is locked."
A few minutes later, Pollyanna was startled awake by Tom shining a lantern in her face.
"Pollyanna!" Aunt Polly cried in astonishment from the attic window. "What are you doing out there?"
Pollyanna blinked and sat up. "I was so hot inside, but don't worry, Aunt Polly. I shut the window after I came out, so flies couldn't carry germs inside."
Tom smiled and quickly disappeared down the ladder.
"Hand those garment bags to me at once and come inside," Aunt Polly said to her niece. To herself she muttered, "Such an unusual child!"
After being outdoors, Pollyanna thought the attic air felt even more stifling. But she didn't complain.
Outside Pollyanna's room Aunt Polly said, "For the rest of the night, you'll sleep in my room. The screens will arrive tomorrow, but until then it's my duty to know where you are."
Pollyanna's eyes widened in delight. "How perfectly lovely! I've always wanted to share a room with someone who belongs to me!"
On the way to her room, Aunt Polly felt both bewildered and helpless. Once again, Pollyanna had turned a punishment into a reward.

In the early days of July, Pollyanna read aloud, studied cooking and sewing, and practiced the piano. But she also had four hours every afternoon to "just live." It was unclear why Pollyanna had been given all this free time. Was Aunt Polly giving her a break from the other activities? Or was Aunt Polly herself taking a break—from Pollyanna?

Either way, Pollyanna enjoyed her afternoons. The Harrington house was on the edge of town, and no children lived nearby. This didn't bother Pollyanna, who enjoyed walking around town, observing people. On these walks, she often ran into a man who was usually alone.
Feeling sorry for him one day, Pollyanna said cheerfully, "How are you, sir? It's a nice day!"
The man glanced around. "Did you just speak to me?"
"Yes, sir, I said—"
The man grunted and walked away.
Pollyanna laughed. "What a funny fellow!"
When she spoke to him the next day, he grunted again. But the third time she greeted him, he stopped abruptly.
"Who are you, and why are you speaking to me?" the man demanded.
"I'm Pollyanna Whittier, and I thought you looked lonely." Pollyanna smiled. "I've told you my name, but I don't know yours."
The man scowled and walked away faster than ever.
Pollyanna's smile faded, but she kept walking. When she arrived home, Nancy was grumbling about doing an errand for Aunt Polly.

"How I hate visiting Mrs. Snow!" Nancy was packing a container of beef stew into a basket. "She complains all the time. Even the days of the week make her unhappy. If it's Tuesday, she wishes it were Wednesday. I feel sorry for her daughter, Milly, who takes care of her."
"Who's Mrs. Snow?" Pollyanna asked.
"An invalid who belongs to Miss Polly's church. Miss Polly thinks it's her duty to send Mrs. Snow some food every week. But she doesn't do it herself—she sends me."
"Mrs. Snow sounds different. I love people who are different! I'll be happy to take the stew to her."
"But you just came home," Nancy protested weakly.
"I'd be glad to go out again." Pollyanna reached for the basket, and Nancy handed it over.
Half an hour later, Pollyanna was standing in Mrs. Snow's darkened bedroom. When her eyes adjusted to the gloom, she saw a woman half–sitting up in bed.
"Hello, Mrs. Snow, I've brought some beef stew from my aunt Polly."
"Beef stew? I'm grateful, of course, but I was hoping for chicken soup today. I didn't sleep a wink last night and—"
"I wish I didn't have to sleep!" Pollyanna sighed. "It's such a waste of time when you could be just living."
The woman sat up straight and peered at Pollyanna. "Aren't you an amazing child! Open the curtains, so I can get a look at you."

"Oh dear, now you'll see my freckles." Pollyanna went over to the window. "Oh!" Pollyanna exclaimed as she turned toward Mrs. Snow. "I'm glad you wanted to see me because now I can see you! Nobody told me you were so pretty."
"Me, pretty?"

"Yes, your eyes are so big and dark, and you have beautiful black curly hair. Let me show you." Pollyanna skipped over to the bureau and picked up a hand mirror. She stopped and studied Mrs. Snow's face.
"If you don't mind, I'd like to fix your hair a little before you look."
"Well, if you must . . ."
"I love to style hair!" Pollyanna fluffed out Mrs. Snow's bangs and arranged her curls. As a finishing touch, she put a pink flower in Mrs. Snow's hair.
Mrs. Snow complained the whole time, but she was secretly excited. At last Pollyanna handed her the mirror.
"I really prefer red flowers." Mrs. Snow frowned. "And my hair will never stay this way."
"Then I'd be glad to come back next week and style it again," Pollyanna said.
"It's hard to be glad about anything when you're stuck in bed all day."
"You're right—that is hard. But I'm sure I'll think of something for you to be glad about." Pollyanna patted Mrs. Snow's arm. "I must go now, but I've had such a lovely time!"
As soon as Pollyanna left, Mrs. Snow looked in the mirror again. "I never realized my hair was so pretty!"
The next time Pollyanna visited Mrs. Snow, the woman was lying in bed with the curtains closed.
"I wish you'd come yesterday," Mrs. Snow said in an irritable voice. "I wanted you yesterday."
"Then I'm glad I'm only a day late," Pollyanna said cheerfully. "It's awfully dark in here."
Pollyanna crossed the room and opened the curtains. "I brought you a surprise and left it with Milly in the kitchen. I'll give you a hint—think of something you'd like."
Mrs. Snow frowned. She was used to saying what she didn't want; she had no idea what she did want.
"Chicken soup?"
"I've got that," Pollyanna said.
"No, I've changed my mind. Lamb stew."
"I've got that and beef stew too! Nancy and I made them all, so you'd have something you like."
Mrs. Snow didn't know how to respond. But that wasn't a problem because Pollyanna went right on talking.
"I've played the game and found something for you to be glad about. It was extra hard because you have to stay in bed. But the game is even more fun when it's hard."
"What game?" Mrs. Snow was puzzled.
"Wait!" Pollyanna took a deep breath. "You can be glad that other people aren't as sick as you are!"
"Well, really!" Mrs. Snow was angry now, but Pollyanna was happily unaware of that.
"I'll tell you about the Glad Game." Pollyanna told the story of wanting a doll but receiving crutches instead.
Just then Milly came in to announce that Miss Polly wanted Pollyanna to hurry home.
"All right." Pollyanna sighed. "I'll hurry." Suddenly she laughed. "I guess I'm glad I have legs to hurry with!"
Mrs. Snow didn't respond, but Milly noticed there were tears on her mother's cheeks.

Although it was raining the next time Pollyanna saw the man, she greeted him with a bright smile. He didn't even bother to grunt in response. Pollyanna assumed he had trouble hearing, so she spoke more loudly the next day.
"I'm glad the sun is shining today, aren't you?" Pollyanna bent down to pat the dog with the man.
The man scowled at her. "I've got other things to think about besides the weather. I don't know whether the sun is shining or not."
Pollyanna smiled brightly. "That's exactly why I mentioned the sun—so you'd notice it! I knew you'd be glad about the sunshine if you stopped to think about it."
The man started to walk away but abruptly turned around to face her again. "Why don't you find someone your own age to talk to?"
"I'd like to, sir, but there's nobody my age around right now. And I like old folks. You see, I'm used to the Ladies' Aid—"
"The Ladies' Aid? Is that what you thought I was?" The man was trying not to smile.
Pollyanna laughed gleefully. "Oh no, sir! You don't look at all like a Ladies' Aider. In fact, I'm sure you're much nicer than you look."
"What?" The man strode away.
But the next time they met, the man spoke to Pollyanna before she could greet him. "Good afternoon! Perhaps I should say right away that I know the sun's shining."
"I knew you knew it as soon as I saw you. I could see it in your eyes and your smile."
"Humph!" grunted the man.
But he continued to talk to Pollyanna whenever they met. One day Nancy happened to be with Pollyanna when the man greeted her.
"Did that man just speak to you?" Nancy's eyes were wide with amazement. "He hasn't spoken to anyone for years."
"He speaks to me, but he's never told me his name."

"That's John Pendleton, and he lives by himself in a mansion on Pendleton Hill. Few people have ever seen inside his house because he doesn't like visitors. He's the richest man in town but doesn't like to spend his money."
"Maybe he's saving it for orphans overseas or something," Pollyanna said.
"I doubt it." Nancy went on. "Everybody thinks he's mysterious. Some years he spends most of his time traveling to faraway places like Egypt."
"He's different," Pollyanna said. "But a different kind of different than Mrs. Snow. I'm gladder than ever that he speaks to me now!"

Throughout July, Pollyanna often told Aunt Polly how happy she was. Aunt Polly usually replied, "It's nice that your days are happy, but that's not enough. They must also be profitable, or I've failed in my duty to you."
Pollyanna answered with hugs and kisses, which Aunt Polly found alarming. But one day during a sewing lesson, Pollyanna asked.
"What does having a 'profitable' day mean?"
"Why, it means having something to show for the day," Aunt Polly said.
"So, just being glad isn't profitable?"
"Certainly not." Aunt Polly rapped her thimble on the table.
"Oh! Then I'm afraid you'll never want to play the game."
"Game? What game?"
"The game that Fath—" Pollyanna clapped her hand over her mouth. "I mean, it's nothing."
"That's enough for this morning," Aunt Polly said, and their sewing lesson was over.
That afternoon Pollyanna was going down the attic stairs when she met Aunt Polly coming up.
"You're coming to see me!" Pollyanna cried with delight. She scampered back up the stairs and threw open her door in welcome.

Aunt Polly had not intended to visit her niece. Instead she'd planned to look for a shawl in the main part of the attic. So she was surprised to find herself sitting in a chair in Pollyanna's room. Then again, she'd often found herself doing surprising things since Pollyanna's arrival.
"I love having visitors!" Pollyanna said. "And I love this room, even though it doesn't have the carpets and curtains and pictures I—" She stopped short.
Her aunt looked at her. "What's that, Pollyanna?"
Pollyanna turned red with embarrassment. "I didn't mean to say that."
"Maybe not." There was a note of coldness in Aunt Polly's voice. "But you did say it, so let's hear the rest."
"It was nothing really, just that I'd been planning on pretty carpets and lace curtains and—"
"Planning on them?" Aunt Polly interrupted sharply.
Pollyanna turned even redder as she tried to apologize.

"It was only because I'd never had pretty things. I mean, we had two rugs from the donation box. But one had ink spots and the other had holes. And Fath—I mean, we had two nice pictures. We sold one though to buy me shoes, and the glass broke on another one."
Aunt Polly listened without interrupting as Pollyanna went on.

"When I walked through your house that first day, I shouldn't have been planning how pretty my room would be. But truly, Aunt Polly, in only a few minutes I was glad that this was my room. I was so glad that the bureau didn't have a mirror because I didn't want to see my freckles! There couldn't be a nicer picture than the view from my window. And you've been so good to me."
Now it was Aunt Polly's turn to blush. She suddenly rose to her feet and said stiffly, "You've said quite enough."
The next minute Aunt Polly swept downstairs, leaving a baffled Pollyanna behind. It was only when Aunt Polly reached the first floor that she realized she'd forgotten the shawl.
In the morning Aunt Polly spoke to Nancy. "Today you may move Miss Pollyanna's things to the room below."
"Yes, ma'am," Nancy said quietly.
A few minutes later, Nancy broke the happy news to Pollyanna in the attic. Nancy gathered up an armload of clothes. "I'll hurry and take your things down before Miss Polly changes her mind."
Pollyanna went flying downstairs, taking the steps two at a time. She banged two doors and knocked over a chair before finding her aunt in the sitting room.
"Oh, Aunt Polly, thank you! That room has everything I ever wanted!"

"I'm glad you like it, and I trust you'll take proper care of everything," Aunt Polly said. "But please pick up that chair, and stop banging doors." She would have said more, but for some strange reason, she felt like crying.
"I'm sorry I banged the doors, but I was just so happy! Did you ever bang doors when you were happy?"
"Certainly not!" Aunt Polly was shocked at the thought.
"Oh, that's a shame because that means you were never glad about something."
Before Aunt Polly could reply, Pollyanna dashed back upstairs to help Nancy move her things.

11.title: A Kitten, a Dog, and a Boy

paragraphs.text: August brought several changes and surprises to Aunt Polly's house. One day, as Pollyanna was walking down the road, she found a kitten. She went door to door, trying to find the kitten's owner. When no one claimed it, she brought it home to Aunt Polly, who was reading in the sitting room.
"I was glad I didn't find the owner because I wanted to keep it," Pollyanna confessed.
Aunt Polly stared in horror at the neglected animal Pollyanna was cradling in her arms. She wasn't fond of cats, not even clean, healthy ones.
"What a dirty beast! I'm sure it's sick and covered with fleas."
"I know." Pollyanna looked tenderly down at the kitten. "The poor thing doesn't understand we're going to keep it."
"What?" Aunt Polly dropped her book, startling the kitten.
"I told everybody you'd let me keep it if I couldn't find its owner. Poor, lonely little thing."
Aunt Polly tried to speak, but once again she had that strange helpless feeling.
"You took me in, so I knew you wouldn't let this kitty hunt for a home," Pollyanna said. "At least I had the Ladies' Aid out West, but the poor kitty has no one." Pollyanna ran happily from the room.
"Pollyanna! Pollyanna! I never said—"
But Pollyanna was already halfway to the kitchen. "Nancy! Come see this sweet kitty that Aunt Polly's letting me keep! I'm naming her Fluffy!"
Aunt Polly gasped with dismay, but she felt powerless to object.

The next day Pollyanna brought home a dog, even dirtier and more forlorn than the kitten. Once again Aunt Polly—who disliked dogs even more than cats—said nothing. How could she protest when Pollyanna saw her as an angel of mercy?

A few days later, Pollyanna found yet another creature for Aunt Polly to take in. That morning Aunt Polly gave Pollyanna a break from sewing, so Pollyanna visited Mrs. Snow. The two had become good friends and often played the Glad Game together. On the way home, Pollyanna spotted a boy sitting by the road, whittling a stick.
"Hello!" Pollyanna said cheerfully.
The boy glanced up but quickly looked away. "Hello yourself."
Although Pollyanna liked adults, she really wanted a friend her own age. So she was determined to make the most of this opportunity.
"My name's Pollyanna Whittier." She plopped onto the grass near the boy. "What's yours?"
"Jimmy Bean."
"Where do you live?"
"Nowhere."
Pollyanna persisted. "Everybody lives somewhere."
"I'm hunting for a new place."
"Oh! Where is it?"
"If I knew where it was, I wouldn't be hunting for it." Jimmy's voice dripped with scorn.
This was not a nice boy, but he was a young person, so Pollyanna tried again.
"Where did you live before?" she asked.
Jimmy shook his head in disbelief. "Do you always ask so many questions?"
"If you'd talk more, I wouldn't have to pester you with questions."

"Okay!" Jimmy smiled slightly. "I'm ten, almost eleven, and I went to live at the Orphans' Home last year. It's so crowded that I left this morning to find a real home. If you have a home, you have a family, and I haven't had one since—" Jimmy sniffed as if trying to hold back tears. "Since Dad died. I tried four houses, but nobody wanted me, even though I volunteered to work. Is that enough information for you?"

"I know just how you feel," Pollyanna said. "After my father died, there was nobody to take me in until Aunt Polly—" She stopped and her face lit up. "Oh! Aunt Polly will be glad to give you a home! Besides me, she's taken in Fluffy and Buffy, and they're only a cat and a dog."
Jimmy's face brightened. "Would she really?"

"She's so good and kind, the nicest lady in the world!" Pollyanna jumped up and started running home. "There's tons of space in her house, though you may have to start out in the attic room. But it's even nicer now with window screens."
Jimmy laughed as they ran together. "I never met anyone who talked so much!"
"You should be glad I do," Pollyanna said. "Because when I'm talking, you don't have to!"
Pollyanna steered Jimmy Bean straight into Aunt Polly's sitting room.

"Oh, Aunt Polly! I have something even nicer than Fluffy and Buffy for you to bring up. A real live boy!" Pollyanna smiled broadly. "He won't mind sleeping in the attic at first, and he says he'll work. But I'll need him most of the time to play with me."
"Pollyanna!" Aunt Polly's face turned white with shock and then red with anger. "Who is this dirty little boy? Where did you find him?"

Jimmy hesitated and looked toward the door, but Pollyanna pressed on. "He is dirty, but I'm sure he'll improve with a bath. Just like Fluffy and Buffy did! He's an orphan, and his name is Jimmy Bean."
"But what is he doing here?"
"I just explained why he's here," Pollyanna said patiently. "Jimmy wants a home and a family. I told him how good you were to Buffy and Fluffy and me. And that you'd take him in too."
Aunt Polly sat down and raised a shaking hand to her throat. The familiar helplessness was threatening to overcome her again. But she suddenly sat up straight.
"Pollyanna, this is the most absurd thing you've done yet," Aunt Polly said. "As if mangy dogs and cats weren't bad enough, you bring home a ragged little beggar who—"

Jimmy's eyes flashed with anger as he confronted Aunt Polly. "I'm not a beggar, and I don't want anything from you!" He stood right in front of her with his hands on his hips. "I'm willing to work, but I wouldn't have come to your old house if this girl hadn't made me. She said you were so good and kind—the nicest lady in the world. She also said you would be glad to have me live here."
As Pollyanna watched helplessly, Jimmy stormed from the room.
"Oh, Aunt Polly, I thought you would be glad to have Jimmy—"
Aunt Polly raised her hand to silence Pollyanna. She felt herself wavering as she remembered Jimmy calling her "good and kind." But then she rallied.
"Pollyanna, please stop using that word glad . All I hear is glad, glad, glad until I can't take it anymore!"
Pollyanna's jaw dropped in amazement. "Why, Aunt Polly, I'd think you'd be glad to have me feel gl—oh!" She broke off suddenly and ran from the room.

Before Jimmy reached the end of the driveway, Pollyanna overtook him. "Wait! I'm so sorry!" Pollyanna was panting as she held out her hand to him. "Please don't blame Aunt Polly—she really is good and kind. It's my fault because I didn't do a good job of introducing you."
"I'm not blaming you." Jimmy shrugged and turned away. "I guess I can find my own place to live. But I'm no beggar!"
"I do wish I could find someplace for you, though." Pollyanna was looking at Jimmy thoughtfully when she suddenly got a bright idea.

"I know what I'll do! The Ladies' Aid meets this afternoon at Aunt Polly's church. I'll tell them all about you." Pollyanna was excited about her plan. "That's what Father always did whenever he wanted anything for his church."
"Oh, no!" Jimmy backed away from Pollyanna. "It's bad enough having one lady call me a beggar. I'm not standing around and listening to a whole room full of ladies call me that."

"But you wouldn't be there. I'd go by myself, and I'd tell your story better this time." Pollyanna kept talking as she sensed Jimmy changing his mind. "I'm sure someone there would be glad to give you a home."
"I'm willing to work," Jimmy reminded her. "Don't forget to say that."
"Of course not. Then tomorrow I'll tell you what happened. I'll meet you on the road where I found you this morning."
Jimmy promised to be there and said he'd decided to return to the Orphans' Home for the night. "Even though I don't think they'd miss me," he added. "They aren't like a family, you know."
"I do know," Pollyanna said sympathetically.

Meanwhile Aunt Polly was watching the children from her sitting room window. She kept remembering Jimmy saying scornfully that she was so good and kind. And Aunt Polly felt sad, as if she'd lost something.
After Jimmy left, Pollyanna and Aunt Polly sat down to lunch. Pollyanna tried to speak, but gave up when she almost said "glad" five times.
Aunt Polly shook her head and sighed. "Just go ahead and say the word, Pollyanna."
"Oh, thank you!" Pollyanna looked up from her soup and smiled. "It's pretty hard not to say it because I've played the game for so long."
"You've what?"
"Played the game that Father . . ." Pollyanna blushed. That was another word she wasn't supposed to say.
Aunt Polly buttered a roll and said nothing. The rest of the meal was silent except for the clinking of silverware on china.

After lunch Pollyanna was playing with Buffy, the dog, when she heard Aunt Polly on the telephone. Aunt Polly was telling someone that she'd be unable to attend the Ladies' Aid meeting because of a headache. Then she went upstairs to her room and closed the door.

"I'm sorry Aunt Polly has a headache," Pollyanna said as she petted Buffy. "But I'm glad she won't be at the meeting this afternoon. I wouldn't want her calling Jimmy 'a little beggar' in front of everyone."

Pollyanna knew that the Ladies' Aid meeting was scheduled for two o'clock in the church social hall. But she had already decided to arrive late. "I want all the ladies to be there before I start talking about Jimmy," she explained to Buffy. "The more people who hear about him, the better."
Buffy wagged his tail in agreement.

Pollyanna left home around half past two. With quiet confidence, she entered the social hall and stood for a moment, listening for voices. Following the sound, she entered a large room filled with ladies. The chatter immediately stopped. Everyone turned to look at Pollyanna, and she suddenly felt shy. These were not her own dear Ladies' Aiders from her church out West, but a group of strangers.
"How do you do, Ladies' Aiders?" Pollyanna said bravely. "I'm Pollyanna Whittier. I guess some of you know me—maybe?"
Pollyanna could feel the silence filling the room. Some of the ladies had met Pollyanna, and almost all of them had heard of her. But no one could think of anything to say to her.

After a moment Pollyanna remembered what she'd heard her father say to the Ladies' Aiders back home. She coughed slightly before addressing them in a clear, loud voice. "I've come to lay a case before you."
There was a slight rustle as the ladies sat up to pay attention.
"Did your aunt send you, my dear?" Mrs. Ford, the minister's wife, asked.
"Oh, no. I came all by myself. You see, I'm used to Ladies' Aiders because they helped Father bring me up."
A few of the ladies raised their eyebrows.
"But why are you here?" Mrs. Ford asked.

"Jimmy Bean hasn't any home except the orphanage, and he doesn't think anyone there really wants him. He'd like a home with a family who'll care about him. He's almost 11, and I thought some of you might want him." Pollyanna paused, hoping someone would speak. "To live with you," she quickly added.
A woman in a red hat finally broke the silence. "Did you ever hear anything like it?" she murmured to the others.
With anxious eyes, Pollyanna examined the faces staring at her.
"Oh, I almost forgot to say that he'll work!" she exclaimed.

A few women questioned Pollyanna, and soon everyone understood what she was asking. Ignoring her, the women talked among themselves. No one wanted to take Jimmy, though some ladies thought others should because they had no sons.
"Perhaps," Mrs. Ford said timidly, "there is something we can do as a group. We could assume responsibility for his care instead of supporting orphanages overseas."
A great many women started talking at once. Pollyanna learned that this group of Ladies' Aiders was famous for donating large amounts of money to orphanages overseas.
The woman in the red hat spoke again. "I would die of embarrassment if we contributed less this year."
Another woman nodded in agreement. "We always top the list of big donors."
Pollyanna said nothing and was soon glad to escape the meeting. "I don't understand why it's more important to top some list than to help Jimmy," she muttered.
After the Ladies' Aid meeting, Pollyanna needed a break. She didn't want to think about her next conversation with Jimmy.
"I don't have to be home until half past five," she said, heading toward Pendleton Hill. "It'll be so much nicer to walk home through Pendleton Woods."
The woods seemed lovelier than usual to Pollyanna. For a few minutes, she was able to forget that none of the ladies had wanted Jimmy. Suddenly a barking dog came dashing down the path toward her.
"Hello, doggie! You belong to Mr. Pendleton!" Pollyanna waited eagerly for the man to appear, but he did not. "Where is he?"
Meanwhile the dog was acting strangely, giving short barks of alarm and running back and forth. Pollyanna followed it down a path that branched off to one side.

"Oh, no!" Pollyanna exclaimed, spotting a man lying motionless at the foot of a rocky ledge. A dead branch cracked sharply under her foot, and the man turned his head toward her. With a cry of dismay, Pollyanna ran to his side.
"Mr. Pendleton! Are you hurt?"

"No, I'm just taking a nap in the woods," he snapped sarcastically but quickly apologized. "I beg your pardon, child. It's just this leg of mine." Mr. Pendleton paused. With some difficulty, he fished a key from his pants pocket and held it out to Pollyanna.

"At the end of this path is my house. This key will unlock the side door. When you get inside, go straight down the hall to the library. On the desk in the middle of the room, you'll find a telephone. Do you know how to use a telephone?"
"Oh, yes, sir! Once when Aunt Polly—"

"Never mind Aunt Polly now." Mr. Pendleton scowled as he struggled to get comfortable. "Look for Dr. Thomas Chilton's phone number in the address book that you'll find somewhere on the desk. You know what an address book is, right?"
"Of course! I just love Aunt Polly's! There are so many names, and—"
"Tell Dr. Chilton that John Pendleton is at the foot of Little Eagle Ledge in Pendleton Woods. Tell him to come at once with a stretcher and two men because I've broken my leg."
"A broken leg? Oh, Mr. Pendleton, how awful!" Pollyanna shuddered. "Is there anything I can do to help?"
"Yes, you can stop talking and do what I asked!" Mr. Pendleton moaned in pain.

With a stifled sob, Pollyanna ran off to get help. It wasn't long before she reached his massive, gray stone house. She sped across the neglected lawn to the side entrance. Pollyanna unlocked the heavy, carved door with the key.

Pollyanna knew she should hurry, but she paused in the hall and glanced around. This was John Pendleton's house, which he never allowed anyone to visit. Yet he expected Pollyanna to enter the dark, spooky place to help him.
"Who knows what's behind all those doors?" Pollyanna said, frightening herself.
Taking a deep breath, she entered the library. Books and papers were strewn across the desk and floor. Everything was covered with dust.

Pollyanna spotted the telephone on the desk, but she had to hunt for the address book. With shaking hands, Pollyanna turned the pages until she found Dr. Chilton's phone number. When he answered the phone, she delivered her message and hung up.
Pollyanna ran back to the woods and sat beside Mr. Pendleton.
"That was quick," he said. "Couldn't you get in?"
"Of course I could! I want to stay with you until Dr. Chilton arrives."
"You could find a nicer person to spend time with than me."
"You mean because you're so grumpy?"
He smiled slightly at her directness. "Yes."
"Oh, you're only grumpy on the outside," Pollyanna said. "Animals always know who's a good, kind person, and your dog is staying right next to you."
Mr. Pendleton reached out and laid a hand on the dog's head.
At last the dog pricked up its ears and barked. Pollyanna looked up as Dr. Chilton arrived with two men and a stretcher.
"I couldn't fix Mr. Pendleton's leg," Pollyanna said to Dr. Chilton, "but I'm glad I found him."
"So am I," Dr. Chilton said, and he turned his attention to the injured man.
Pollyanna was late for supper that night, but it didn't matter. While Pollyanna was out, Aunt Polly had received a telegram that her cousin had died.
"Your aunt left right away for the funeral in Boston," Nancy explained. "I guess we can be glad she'll be gone for three days."
"Oh, no, there are some things—like funerals—that you can't play the game with! Now let me tell you why I'm late."
Soon Nancy was listening in amazement as Pollyanna described Mr. Pendleton's accident and how she'd helped him.
The next day Pollyanna met Jimmy by the side of the road. She explained to the disappointed boy that the Ladies' Aiders preferred to help overseas orphans.
He kicked a stone down the road. "Wouldn't it be great if somebody far away wanted me?"
Pollyanna clapped her hands with glee. "I'll write to my Ladies' Aiders out West. They're so far away that maybe they'll want you!"
"Don't forget to say that I'll work," Jimmy reminded her.
About a week later, Pollyanna went into the sitting room to see Aunt Polly, who was back from Boston.
"Aunt Polly, would you mind if I took Mrs. Snow's beef stew to someone else this week?"
Aunt Polly looked up from her knitting. "What are you up to now, Pollyanna?"

"Nothing you could possibly object to." Pollyanna came over and sat on the footstool near Aunt Polly's chair. "You let me take stew to her , so I thought you'd let me take it to him . You see, his broken leg will be a problem for only a few weeks. But Mrs. Snow is a lifelong invalid. There will be plenty of opportunities to take her stew every week."
"Him? His broken leg? What on earth are you talking about?"

"It all happened while you were away." Pollyanna got a faraway look in her eyes as she recalled that day. "I found him in the woods and had to unlock his house and call the doctor. Of course, then I came home, and I haven't seen him since. But Nancy was making beef stew this morning. And I thought it would be nice to take it to him. May I, Aunt Polly?"
"Yes, I suppose so." Aunt Polly sighed. She sometimes felt worn down by conversations with Pollyanna. "Who did you say he was?"
"Mr. John Pendleton."
Aunt Polly sprang from her chair. "John Pendleton!"
"Yes, Nancy told me his name. Maybe you know him?"
Aunt Polly didn't answer but quietly sat down. "Do you know him?"
"Oh, yes. He always smiles and speaks to me now. He's only grumpy on the outside, you know." Pollyanna stood up. "I'll go and get the stew from Nancy."
Pollyanna was halfway across the room when Aunt Polly stopped her.
"Wait! I've changed my mind." Aunt Polly's voice was suddenly stern. "I'd prefer that Mrs. Snow have that stew today as usual."
Pollyanna's disappointment was clear. "But I want to bring Mr. Pendleton the stew before he gets better. And he's already had a broken leg for a whole week."
"I do not want to send him stew." Aunt Polly shook her head to emphasize the " not ."

Pollyanna was not yet ready to give up. "I understand why you don't like him—he can be awfully grumpy sometimes. But how about this? I won't tell him that you sent the beef stew. I'd be glad to say it was from me."
Aunt Polly started to shake her head again but stopped. She asked in a curiously quiet voice, "Does he know who you are?"
Pollyanna sighed. "I don't think so. I told him my name once, but he never uses it."
"Does he know where you live or that you're my niece?"
"Oh, no. I never told him those things."
For a moment there was silence as Aunt Polly stared blankly into space. Pollyanna waited impatiently, shifting from one foot to the other. At last Aunt Polly spoke.
"Very well, you may take the stew to Mr. Pendleton as your own gift. But let's be perfectly clear about one thing: I didn't send it. Don't let him think that I did!"
"Yes, ma'am. No, ma'am. Thank you, Aunt Polly!" Pollyanna exclaimed as she flew from the room.

Mr. Pendleton's house looked quite different from the last time Pollyanna was there. Every window was open, and the doctor's carriage was outside. Leaving her stew in the kitchen, Pollyanna followed a maid down the hall. They passed Dr. Chilton and a male nurse, who was surprised Dr. Chilton was permitting a visitor.
"I thought Mr. Pendleton didn't want visitors," the nurse said to Dr. Chilton.
"If anyone can improve his mood, it's that child."
"Who is she?"
The doctor hesitated. "Pollyanna Whittier is the niece of a prominent Beldingsville resident. I don't know Pollyanna well, but many of my patients do. She does them more good than some medicines!"
The nurse smiled. "What's her secret ingredient?"
"An overwhelming gladness about everything. I wish I could prescribe her to all my patients," Dr. Chilton joked.
Meanwhile, as Pollyanna and the maid passed the library, Pollyanna noticed how clean it was. The maid opened a door, and Pollyanna entered a room. Mr. Pendleton was inside, lying in bed.
"I said I didn't want—," Mr. Pendleton began in an angry voice. "Oh, it's you!" He almost smiled when he spotted Pollyanna.
"I'm so glad to see you!" Pollyanna rushed to his side.
"Well, I'm not glad to be stuck in bed with a broken leg."
"At least you can be glad you didn't break both legs."
"Yes, I'm lucky," the man said sarcastically. "I should be glad I'm not a centipede with a hundred broken legs."
"Oh, that's a good one!" Pollyanna laughed, and Mr. Pendleton found himself smiling despite himself. But his mood soon soured again.
"I hate having all these people in my house and needing to pay them too!"
"Yes, Nancy told me you don't like spending money. I guess you're saving it for orphans overseas."
"What are you talking about? Who's Nancy?"
"Nancy works for my aunt, Polly Harrington. After my father died, Aunt Polly took me in. My mother was her sister Jennie."
Mr. Pendleton groaned and closed his eyes. He looked so upset that Pollyanna was frightened.
"Maybe I should go now," she said. "Enjoy the stew I've brought!"
"Wait!" Mr. Pendleton opened his eyes and gazed fondly at Pollyanna. "So, you're Miss Polly's niece. I can't believe she sent me stew."
"Oh, no, sir!" Pollyanna said with alarm. "She said I must be sure not to let you think that."
"Never mind!" the man snapped and turned away.
Pollyanna tiptoed from the room and found Dr. Chilton waiting to offer her a ride home.
"I love to ride!" Pollyanna beamed at the doctor as they drove away.
"From what I've heard, you love most things."
Pollyanna laughed. "That's true, but mostly I love just living. Of course, Aunt Polly says my days must also be profitable."
"That sounds like something she'd say." Dr. Chilton looked so sad that Pollyanna wished she could do something for him. They rode in silence until Pollyanna was almost home.
"Dr. Chilton," Pollyanna finally said, "I think you're in the gladdest business of all."
The doctor turned to her in surprise. "How can you say that when I see so many people suffering every day?"
"Because you're helping them, and you're glad to help them. So that makes you the gladdest person in Beldingsville."

Dr. Chilton looked away as his eyes filled with tears. He led a lonely life with no wife and no real home. He lived in his two-room office in a boardinghouse. But this little girl had made him appreciate his work.
"Thank you for saying that, Pollyanna. Today the doctor needed some of your medicine too."
"My medicine?" Pollyanna asked.
But they'd arrived at Aunt Polly's, and Dr. Chilton was suddenly eager to be on his way.
Pollyanna found Aunt Polly looking out the sitting room window.
"Why were you in Dr. Chilton's carriage?" she demanded.
"He offered me a ride home from Mr. Pendleton's." Pollyanna couldn't understand why Aunt Polly was annoyed. But Pollyanna could try to cheer her up. "I told Mr. Pendleton you didn't send the stew."
Aunt Polly scolded Pollyanna. "I said you should be sure he didn't think I sent it. Which is far different from telling him that I didn't send it."
"I don't see any difference," Pollyanna said as she went to hang up her hat.
It was raining the next time Aunt Polly attended a Ladies' Aid meeting. When she came home, her face was flushed, and her hair was damp and windblown.
"Oh, Aunt Polly, you look lovely! I didn't know your hair curled in the rain."
Aunt Polly tried to smooth her hair.
"No, don't do that!" Pollyanna cried.
But Aunt Polly had another topic to discuss besides hair. "Why did you go to the Ladies' Aid meeting to talk about that little beggar boy? I was so embarrassed when they told me this afternoon!"

"I didn't know the ladies would be more concerned with orphans overseas than Jimmy," Pollyanna burst out. "Or I would have stayed home. But I've written to my Ladies' Aid out West about taking him. So now we'll just have to wait and see what happens." She paused for a breath. "Oh, please may I fix your hair like I did Mrs. Snow's? You'd look so pretty!"
"Pollyanna!" Aunt Polly scolded, but she was secretly pleased. It had been a long time since anyone had told her that she was pretty.
"You didn't say I couldn't do it!" Pollyanna cried as she ran for the stairs. "Let's go upstairs."
"But, Pollyanna, the Ladies' Aid . . ." Aunt Polly had that helpless feeling again as she trailed upstairs after her niece.
The next thing Aunt Polly knew, she was sitting at the dressing table in her room. Pollyanna began styling her hair.
"Turn so you can't see yourself in the mirror," Pollyanna said before leaving the room. A moment later she returned with a handkerchief that she slipped over Aunt Polly's eyes.
"What are you doing?" Aunt Polly cried.

Pollyanna giggled as she pinned a lacy shawl around Aunt Polly's shoulders. Then she remembered the rosebush that climbed the trellis outside her bedroom window. Aunt Polly tried to resist as Pollyanna pulled her down the hall.
"Where are you taking me?" Aunt Polly said.

"You'll see." Pollyanna leaned out her window and plucked a red rose, which she tucked behind Aunt Polly's ear. She removed the blindfold and held up a hand mirror. "Aren't you glad I dressed you up?"
Aunt Polly took in her surroundings and her own reflection. Then she gave a startled yelp and fled to her room. At that moment Pollyanna saw a carriage coming up the driveway.
"Dr. Chilton!" she called with delight from the window. "Are you looking for me?"
"Yes, will you come outside?"
Rushing into Aunt Polly's room, Pollyanna found her flushed and angry. Aunt Polly was pulling the pins from the shawl.
"Pollyanna, how could you do this to me? You dressed me up, and then . . ." Aunt Polly shook her head in horror. "Let me be seen !"
"But you looked perfectly lovely, Aunt Polly."
"Lovely!" Aunt Polly said scornfully. She flung the shawl aside and attacked her hair with shaking fingers.
"Oh, Aunt Polly, please let your hair stay!"
"Absolutely not!" Aunt Polly pulled her hair back so tightly that not a single curl remained.
"But you looked so pretty!" Pollyanna was almost sobbing as she left the room.
She went outside, where Dr. Chilton was waiting in his carriage. "Mr. Pendleton would like to see you now," he said. "Can you come with me?"
Pollyanna was suddenly cheered up. "Let me ask Aunt Polly." She returned a few moments later, looking serious.
"What's the matter?" Dr. Chilton asked as Pollyanna climbed in.
"Aunt Polly doesn't want anything to do with me right now."
The doctor hesitated. "Was that your aunt I saw with you at the window?"
Pollyanna nodded and took a deep breath. "That's the whole trouble. I fixed her hair, and she looked so pretty. Didn't you think she looked lovely?"
The doctor replied so quietly that Pollyanna could barely hear him. "Yes, I thought she looked lovely."
"Oh, I'm glad!" Pollyanna looked happy again. "I'll be sure to tell her."
"No!" To Pollyanna's alarm, Dr. Chilton was almost shouting. "Don't ever tell her that!"
"Why? I'd think you'd be glad—"
"But she might not be."
Pollyanna considered this for a moment before nodding in agreement. "After all, she ran because she spotted you."
"That's what I thought," Dr. Chilton said softly.
"I'll come back to take you home at half-past five," Dr. Chilton said, leaving Pollyanna at Mr. Pendleton's door.
Pollyanna entered the great stone house and found Mr. Pendleton lying in bed as before. But this time he smiled when she sat down.

"You must be a very forgiving person to visit after the way I've treated you," Mr. Pendleton said. "I apologize for my rudeness when you brought the beef stew. And I've never thanked you for helping me when I broke my leg. Thank you!"
"I was glad to help you," Pollyanna said. "I mean, I wasn't glad your leg was broken."
"I understand what you meant." Mr. Pendleton smiled again. "You were brave that day in the woods, and the stew was delicious. Is there any more today that Aunt Polly didn't send?"
Pollyanna's eyes widened at the reminder of Aunt Polly's scolding. "No, sir."

Mr. Pendleton stared straight ahead, lost in thought. At last he sighed. "I didn't send for you to watch me mope. Go into the library—you know, the big room with the telephone. You'll find a wooden box in the cabinet with glass doors. Bring it here, please."

A few minutes later, Pollyanna returned with the box. It was full of interesting things that Mr. Pendleton had picked up during his travels. He had an entertaining story about every item, including an intricately carved chess set. They also talked about Pollyanna's life with Aunt Polly as well as her former home out West. Much too soon, it was time for Pollyanna to leave.

"I want you to visit me often," Mr. Pendleton said. "I'm lonely, and there's another reason . . ." His voice trailed off. "When I first learned who you are, I didn't want to see you again. You reminded me of something I've tried to forget for years. But then the more I tried to forget, the more I remembered. So now I want you to come. Will you?"
"Of course, Mr. Pendleton." Pollyanna's eyes were filled with sympathy for the sad-faced man.
That evening after supper, Pollyanna sat in the backyard, talking with Nancy.
"I can't believe Mr. Pendleton showed you all those things and told you stories about them." Nancy shook her head in amazement. "He's usually so grumpy—if he even bothers to speak."
Pollyanna quickly defended her new friend. "People wouldn't think he's so bad if they knew him."
Nancy swatted away a fly. "I don't understand why he's so interested in you. I mean, no offense, but he's not someone who likes children."
Pollyanna smiled. "He didn't like me right away. Just today he admitted that, at first, he didn't want to see me again. I reminded him of something he wanted to forget and—"
"Something he wanted to forget?" Nancy leaned forward with excitement. "What was it?"
"He didn't say."
"A mystery!" Nancy said in an awestruck voice. "Just like in the mystery novels I love to read. Only this is a real-life mystery! Tell me every little detail."
So Pollyanna told everything she could remember from the first time she met Mr. Pendleton until that day.
"He didn't want to see you again after he learned you were Miss Polly's niece, right?" Nancy said.
"Yes, that's what he said today."
"And he acted strange when you said Miss Polly didn't want him to think she'd sent the stew?" Nancy was growing more excited by the minute.
"Yes, but—"
"I've got it!" Nancy looked around to make sure nobody else was listening. "He and Miss Polly were sweethearts!"
"What? Aunt Polly doesn't even like him. She didn't want him to think the beef stew came from her."
"Tom told me that she had a sweetheart long ago. They had an argument and broke off their engagement. Tom said the man still lives in town!"
Pollyanna still wasn't convinced, so Nancy pressed on. "Mr. Pendleton said you reminded him of someone. It has to be Miss Polly!"
"But if they loved each other, they would have made up years ago."
"Sometimes sweethearts can be stubborn." Nancy had a dreamy look on her face. "Wouldn't it be wonderful if you taught them the Glad Game and they got back together?"
During August, Pollyanna often visited Mr. Pendleton, but she wasn't sure how much her visits helped him.
"He seems to like to hear me talk," she thought one afternoon as she walked home through Pendleton Woods. She smiled. "And I do like to talk!"
But she had trouble predicting which topics would upset him. Today she had tried to tell him about the Glad Game, but he cut her off when she mentioned her father.

Pollyanna remembered Nancy's idea that Mr. Pendleton and Aunt Polly had been engaged. "I'm beginning to think Nancy was right. Sometimes he's interested in what I say about Aunt Polly; other times he gets irritable. But he always listens with a strange smile on his face."

Pollyanna stopped to watch two squirrels chasing each other. "Oh, I wish I could bring Aunt Polly and Mr. Pendleton together! They're both so lonely, but I don't know how to help them. Aunt Polly never wants to hear what I have to say about him. Then again, she never wants to hear about Dr. Chilton either. But that's probably because he saw her dressed up with the rose and shawl."
Later that week Pollyanna again noticed Aunt Polly's dislike of Dr. Chilton. Pollyanna was in bed with a bad cold.
"If you aren't better by tonight, I'm sending for the doctor," Aunt Polly said.
"Then I hope I get worse." Pollyanna giggled. "I'd love to have Dr. Chilton visit."
"Dr. Chilton is not our family physician," Aunt Polly said firmly. "I'll ask Dr. Warren to come."
"I like Dr. Warren, but I like Dr. Chilton better. And Dr. Chilton would feel hurt if I didn't use him. It wasn't his fault that he saw you looking so pretty."
"That will do, Pollyanna. I do not wish to discuss Dr. Chilton or his feelings."
Pollyanna studied her aunt's face. "I'd love to fix your hair again, Aunt Polly. Wait—"
But Aunt Polly had already left Pollyanna's room. That evening there was no need to summon a doctor.
After Pollyanna had recovered, she paid another visit to Mr. Pendleton. Upon entering his room, she cried, "There's a rainbow on your pillow! How did it get inside the house?"
"Do you see that thermometer hanging outside the window?" Mr. Pendleton pointed. "Sunlight striking its glass edge causes a prism effect."
"Oh, that's so beautiful! I wish I could live in a rainbow."
Mr. Pendleton laughed as he watched Pollyanna happily studying the colors. "Let's see what we can do about that."
He touched a bell beside his bed, and the maid soon appeared. "Bring me a brass candlestick from the drawing room mantel."
As the maid returned, Pollyanna heard tinkling. She noticed glass pendants hanging from the candlestick. "Oh, those pendants are making such a pretty musical sound!"
Mr. Pendleton asked the maid to remove a curtain and stretch a string across the window. Then he slipped a dozen pendants from the candlestick.
"Now, Pollyanna, hook these glass pieces onto the string. If you really want to live in a rainbow, we'll make one for you."
Pollyanna hung three pendants in the sunlit window. She was so excited that her hands trembled and she could barely finish the job. At last she stepped back to admire her work.

"It's like a fairyland!" she cried. The entire room was aglow with shimmering bits of color. "Perhaps the sun is trying to play the game! Oh, I wish I had prisms to give to Mrs. Snow and lots of folks. Nancy's birthday is next week. And they'd make Aunt Polly so glad, she'd bang doors."
Mr. Pendleton laughed. "It would take more than prisms to make your aunt do that. But what is this game you mentioned?"

Pollyanna explained the game and told him the story of the doll and crutches. This time he didn't mind hearing about her father. Tears came to his eyes. "I think you're the finest prism of all," he said.
"No, beautiful colors don't shine through me. The sun just gives me freckles."
Mr. Pendleton laughed, but Pollyanna thought it sounded more like a sob.
He pressed the bell to summon the maid again. "Pollyanna, I'm sending you home with prisms for you and your friends. And a gold coin for Nancy's birthday."
"Oh, thank you, sir!"

In September, Pollyanna started school in Beldingsville. She quickly made many friends among the boys and girls in her class. Much to her surprise, she actually enjoyed her schoolwork. Although she was a happy student, she didn't forget her old friends. She continued to visit Mrs. Snow and Mr. Pendleton on a regular basis.
Mr. Pendleton, however, was not happy and complained to her one Saturday afternoon. "I rarely see you these days," he said as they sat in his library. "How would you like to come live with me?"
Pollyanna thought he was joking. "Oh, Mr. Pendleton, you're so funny! I thought you didn't like having people in your house."

"That was before you taught me to play your wonderful game. Now I'm glad to have people here to help me. Not that I'll need them forever. I'll soon be up and walking around as usual. Then, watch out!" He playfully shook one of his crutches at her.
Pollyanna frowned at him. "But you aren't really glad about things; you just say you are. You know, you never play the game the right way."
Mr. Pendleton looked very serious. "That's why I want you to live with me—to help me play it. So will you come?"
"Mr. Pendleton, you don't really mean that."
"Yes, I do."
When Pollyanna realized he was serious, she felt upset. "You know I can't. I'm Aunt Polly's!"
He spoke with a sudden fierceness. "You're no more hers than . . ." His voice grew gentler. "I mean, perhaps she'd allow you to live here. Would you come, if she let you?"
"But Aunt Polly has been so good to me," Pollyanna said slowly. "She took me in when I didn't have anybody left but the Ladies' Aid and—"
A spasm crossed Mr. Pendleton's face as if he was in pain.
"Pollyanna, a long time ago, I loved somebody very much. I had hoped to bring her to this house someday. I imagined how happy we'd be here and that we'd spend the rest of our lives together."
"Go on." Pollyanna encouraged him, her eyes full of sympathy.

"But . . . well . . . I didn't bring her here. Never mind why. I just didn't, that's all." Mr. Pendleton gazed out the window for a moment before returning his focus to Pollyanna. "Ever since then, this great, gray pile of stone has been a house but never a home. I think it takes a spouse's hand and heart to make a house a home. Or else a child's presence, and I haven't had that either. Now that you've heard my story, Pollyanna, won't you come and turn this house into a home?"
Pollyanna sprang to her feet, her face bright with joy. "Do you wish you'd had that woman's hand and heart all this time?"
Mr. Pendleton nodded.
"Oh, I'm so glad!" She sighed contentedly. "You can take us both, and everything will be all right."
"Take you both?" Mr. Pendleton was puzzled.
"Well, Aunt Polly isn't persuaded yet. But I'm sure she will be, if you tell your story the same way you told me. Then we'll both come live with you!"
A look of terror filled Mr. Pendleton's eyes. "Aunt Polly come . . . here ?"
"Unless you'd rather go there? Her house isn't quite as pretty as yours, but it's—"
"Pollyanna, stop! What are you talking about?"
"Where we're going to live, of course." Surprised by his question, Pollyanna went on. "You said you wanted Aunt Polly's hand and heart years ago to make a home and—"
A cry came from Mr. Pendleton's throat. Before he could speak, the maid suddenly appeared in the doorway.
"Dr. Chilton is here," she announced.
Pollyanna rose to leave.
"Say nothing about what I asked you," Mr. Pendleton begged Pollyanna in a quiet voice.
Pollyanna broke into a grin and called back over her shoulder. "Of course not. I know you'd rather ask Aunt Polly yourself!"
Mr. Pendleton fell back limply in his chair and tried to breathe calmly.
"What's the matter?" Dr. Chilton rushed to Mr. Pendleton's side and felt his racing pulse.
Mr. Pendleton managed a smile. "Too much of that medicine you prescribed!"
The next day Pollyanna went to Sunday school after the church service. As she started to walk home, she spotted Dr. Chilton. He offered her a ride.
"Mr. Pendleton wants you to visit him this afternoon," Dr. Chilton said as Pollyanna settled into the carriage. "He said it was very important."
