Pollyanna nodded. "Yes, I'll be there."
"You seemed to upset my patient yesterday." The doctor's eyes twinkled. "I'm not sure you should go after all."
Pollyanna laughed. "Oh, it wasn't me. It was Aunt Polly."
"Your aunt!" Dr. Chilton said.

Pollyanna bounced on the seat. "It's so exciting, just like a story in a book. Mr. Pendleton said not to mention it, but he won't mind if you know. He meant I shouldn't mention it to Aunt Polly. Of course, he'll want to tell her himself because that's what sweethearts do."
"Sweethearts!" At that word the horse started violently, as if Dr. Chilton had jerked the reins.
"Yes, Nancy told me that Aunt Polly had a sweetheart years ago. But they quarreled and broke off their engagement. We just figured out who Aunt Polly's sweetheart is. It's Mr. Pendleton!"
"Really? I hadn't heard that." Dr. Chilton looked amused.

They were almost at the Harrington house, so Pollyanna hurried to finish. "I'm so glad now. Everything has turned out perfectly just like in a book. Mr. Pendleton asked me to come live with him. But I can't leave Aunt Polly after all she's done for me. Then he told me about the woman he used to love and that he still loves her. So Aunt Polly and I will go live with him, or he'll come live with us."
Pollyanna paused for breath. "We haven't got everything settled yet, so I suppose that's why he wants to see me later."
"Hmm, yes, well, here we are at your house." Dr. Chilton pulled his horse to a stop.
"There's Aunt Polly in the window!" Pollyanna cried. "Oh, now I don't see her."
The doctor was no longer smiling.
That afternoon Pollyanna found a nervous Mr. Pendleton waiting in his library.
"I've been thinking about this ever since you left yesterday," he said. "Why did you say I wanted Aunt Polly's hand and heart years ago?"
"Because you were sweethearts! And I was so glad you still felt that way."
"Sweethearts? Your aunt and me?"
Pollyanna was startled by the surprise in his voice. "Nancy said you were."
"Nancy was wrong."
"You mean, you weren't engaged?" Pollyanna said with dismay.
"Never." Mr. Pendleton stared out the window.
"But everything was working out perfectly just like in a book." Pollyanna was on the verge of tears. "I'd have been glad to live here—with Aunt Polly."
Mr. Pendleton didn't look at Pollyanna. "Does that mean you won't come now?"
"I can't. I'm Aunt Polly's."
The man turned toward Pollyanna and said fiercely, "Before you were hers, you were your mother's. And it was your mother's hand and heart that I wanted years ago."
"My mother's?" Pollyanna blinked. She couldn't believe what she was hearing.

"I loved your mother, but she didn't love me. Instead she married your father, and my whole world collapsed. I became a grumpy, unlovable, unloved old man—although I'm not yet sixty. Then one day you danced into this gray, stone house like a colorful prism. At first, I couldn't stand to be reminded of your mother, but that's changed. Now I'm begging you to let me adopt you."
Pollyanna's eyes blurred with tears. "But, Mr. Pendleton, what about Aunt Polly?"
Mr. Pendleton gestured impatiently. "What about me? How can I be glad without you? I'll spend every last cent of my money on your happiness."
Pollyanna looked shocked. "But you've saved your money for the orphans overseas."
"I never . . ."
Pollyanna didn't notice that Mr. Pendleton had tried to speak. "And you make people like Mrs. Snow and Nancy glad with your gifts," she went on.
Mr. Pendleton shook his head. "Prisms and a gold coin—they're nothing. And Miss Polly doesn't need you as much as I do."
"I know she's glad—"
"Miss Polly doesn't know how to be glad about anything. She only knows how to do her duty. Please, just ask if she'll let you live here."
Pollyanna promised to ask, but she wasn't very glad about it!
Pollyanna left Mr. Pendleton's house. As she walked down Pendleton Hill, the sky was filled with storm clouds. Soon she met Nancy carrying an umbrella.
"Miss Polly was worried you'd get soaked in the rain."
"Oh, I didn't mean to scare her."
"Well, I'm glad she was worried," Nancy said.
Pollyanna was so shocked, she stopped walking. " Glad that Aunt Polly was worried about me? Oh, Nancy, that's not how we play the game."

"I wasn't playing the game," Nancy said sharply. "You don't appreciate what it means that Miss Polly was worried about you. It means she's becoming human! She's not just doing her duty all the time. And she's a better person since you arrived. She took in that dog and cat, and she's much nicer to me."
Pollyanna hesitated. "Do you think Aunt Polly likes that I live with her? Would she miss me if I left?"
"Of course she'd miss you! She sent me out with this umbrella. And she moved you to that pretty bedroom."
Nancy knew her words would please Pollyanna. But she wasn't prepared for the sudden joy that illuminated Pollyanna's face.

Pollyanna skipped the rest of the way home. "I couldn't leave Aunt Polly now," she thought. "I always knew I wanted to live with her. But I didn't know how much I wanted Aunt Polly to want to live with me!"

The next day Pollyanna walked back up Pendleton Hill. She dreaded telling Mr. Pendleton of her decision to stay with Aunt Polly. She felt sorry that he lived such a sad, lonely life. And she suspected that the big, gray house would become cluttered and dusty again.
"If only there was someone else . . . Oh, I have an idea!"
She hurried into Mr. Pendleton's library, where a cheery fire glowed in the fireplace.
"I've thought of the gladdest thing you could do!"
"With you?" Mr. Pendleton said cautiously.
"No, but—"
"You're turning down my offer?"
Pollyanna nodded. "Aunt Polly—"
"Did she refuse to let you come?"
"I—I didn't ask her. I couldn't ask her after I accidentally found out she wants me with her. And I want to stay too. She's starting to be glad about a lot of things, so I can't leave her now."
There was a long pause with only the crackling fire to break the silence.
"I'm disappointed, but I won't ask you again." Mr. Pendleton spoke in a low voice.
"I have a new idea! You want a partner's hand and heart or a child's presence to make this house a home. Well, I know another child you could adopt!"
Mr. Pendleton looked outraged by her suggestion. "I don't want another child."
"But you're so kind to other people. You gave prisms to Mrs. Snow and me, a gold coin to Nancy, money to orphans overseas."
"Pollyanna, listen!" Mr. Pendleton said sharply. "I've never sent a penny to orphans overseas, and those other gifts were your ideas."

Mr. Pendleton expected Pollyanna to be disappointed in him. Instead she gleefully clapped her hands. "I'm so glad! I mean, I'm not glad that you've sent nothing to the orphans. But I'm glad you can help Jimmy Bean."
"Who's Jimmy Bean?"
"The 'child's presence' that's going to make this place a home. Poor Jimmy! I had to tell him that my Ladies' Aid out West wouldn't take him. He'll be so glad to come here!"
"Pollyanna, this is nonsense!"
"You mean you won't take him?" Pollyanna was stunned.
"Correct."
"Fine! I'll find someone else who wants a nice little boy." Tears of frustration streamed down Pollyanna's face. "I didn't even get to say he's willing to work."
Moved by her tears, Mr. Pendleton spoke gently. "Why don't you tell me more about this nice little boy?"

The next Saturday Pollyanna and Jimmy visited Mr. Pendleton. Jimmy was wary about meeting another of Pollyanna's friends. Having been rejected by Aunt Polly and two Ladies' Aid groups, he wasn't exactly rude. But when Mr. Pendleton asked him questions, he looked away and gave short answers. He never once smiled or thanked Mr. Pendleton for inviting him to visit.
After Jimmy left, Pollyanna turned to Mr. Pendleton. "So, are you going to adopt him?"
"I'll think about it," Mr. Pendleton replied.
Pollyanna sighed. That probably meant no.
A few days later, Pollyanna brought Fluffy to visit Mrs. Snow. While they were having fun watching the cat play, Mrs. Snow suddenly remembered something important.

"Milly is doing errands, and I meant to ask her to stop by Dr. Chilton's," Mrs. Snow said. "He prescribed a new medicine for me. But I can't remember the name or how many times a day to take it. Oh, dear! What am I going to do?"
Pollyanna hopped up, eager to help. "I'd be glad to run over to his office and ask him."
"That would be wonderful!"
Pollyanna was happy to be outside on such a beautiful day. When she reached Dr. Chilton's office, he welcomed her at the door.
"Pollyanna, your timing is perfect," Dr. Chilton said. "I've just seen my last patient of the day. What can I do for you?"
"Mrs. Snow can't remember the name of the medicine you told her to buy. She also needs to know how often to take it."
"Come in, and I'll write that down for her." Dr. Chilton beckoned Pollyanna inside and sat down at his desk.

Pollyanna looked around the room while he wrote a note on a pad of paper. Besides Dr. Chilton's desk, the room contained several chairs as well as a bookcase filled with medical texts. Through an open door, Pollyanna spotted an examining table and a glass-front cabinet. It contained a microscope and a model of the human body. There were also a chest and a cot. Everything appeared neat and well-organized.
"I've never been inside your home before," Pollyanna said. "This is your home as well as your office, right?"
"Yes, but it's a poor excuse for a home. These are just rooms. They aren't really a home."
Pollyanna nodded in sympathy. "Yes, I've heard someone say it takes a spouse's hand and heart or a child's presence to make a house a home."
"What?" The doctor spun around in his chair.

"That's what Mr. Pendleton told me." Pollyanna paused. "Why don't you get a woman's hand and heart, Dr. Chilton? Or maybe you'd take Jimmy Bean, if Mr. Pendleton doesn't want him. Jimmy's a really nice orphan, and he's willing to work too. But I'm not sure he made the best impression on Mr. Pendleton."
Dr. Chilton gave a slight smile as he turned back toward his desk. "So Mr. Pendleton thinks it takes a spouse's hand and heart to make a home?"
"Yes, he says his mansion is just a house too. So why don't you, Dr. Chilton?"
"Why don't I what?"

"Get a woman's hand and heart. Oh, I almost forgot to tell you! It wasn't Aunt Polly who Mr. Pendleton loved long ago, so we aren't going to live with him. I made a mistake when I told you it was Aunt Polly." Pollyanna looked anxious. "I hope you didn't tell anyone."
"No, I didn't tell anyone."
Pollyanna sighed with relief. "Oh, then it's all right. But you still haven't answered my question. Why don't you get a spouse?"
Dr. Chilton was silent for a few moments before he said in a serious voice, "You can't always get a spouse just by asking."
Pollyanna studied the doctor. "But I would think you'd be able to get one. Lots of women would be glad to marry you."
Dr. Chilton raised his eyebrows and laughed. "I'm afraid some women aren't as confident about that as you are, young lady."
Pollyanna's eyes widened in surprise. "Wait a minute! Are you like Mr. Pendleton? Did you try to get someone's hand and heart, and she turned you down?"
"I'd do anything to have one particular woman's hand and heart." Dr. Chilton spoke so softly that Pollyanna had to strain to hear him.
"What did you say?" she asked.

Dr. Chilton abruptly stood up. "There, there, Pollyanna. Never mind about that now. Don't bother yourself with other people's troubles. It's time for you to run back to Mrs. Snow. I've written down the name of the medicine and directions for taking it. Was there anything else she needed?"
Pollyanna shook her head. "No, sir. Thank you, sir." And she hurried back to Mrs. Snow and Fluffy.

On the last day of October, a terrible accident occurred. Pollyanna was walking home from school when a speeding car hit her. The driver fled, and no one witnessed the accident. Luckily, a neighbor soon came upon the unconscious girl. He carried her home, where a frightened Aunt Polly and sobbing Nancy gently put her to bed.
When Dr. Warren arrived, Nancy ran to tell Tom, who was raking leaves.
Tom dropped his rake. "Is she seriously injured?" His voice shook.
"I don't know!" Nancy sobbed. "She has a little cut on her head, but Miss Polly's afraid Pollyanna has internal injuries. You know, Miss Polly really loves that girl."
Nancy ran back into the house to wait for the doctor's diagnosis. But all she overheard was that Pollyanna had no broken bones and a nurse would arrive that night.
Later Nancy and Tom were eating supper in the kitchen.
"Dr. Warren sounded very serious and said, 'only time will tell,'" Nancy said. "What does that mean?"
Tom sighed. "It means we have to wait."
The next morning Pollyanna woke up.
"Aunt Polly! Why are you sitting by my bed? I need to get ready for school." When Pollyanna tried to sit up, she fell back on her pillow and moaned. "Why can't I get up?"
"I wouldn't try just yet, dear," Aunt Polly said in a soothing voice.
"What's the matter with me?"
Aunt Polly gave an agonized look at the nurse standing at the window. The young woman nodded and whispered, "Tell her."
Aunt Polly cleared her throat. "You were hurt by a car yesterday. But don't think about that now."
"Hurt? Oh, yes, I walked . . ." Pollyanna brushed a hand across her forehead. "There's a bandage on my head . . . and it hurts!"
"Yes, dear, just try to rest."
"But, Aunt Polly, my legs feel so . . . so odd. I can't really feel them."
Aunt Polly struggled to her feet and gave the nurse a look, begging for help.
The nurse approached Pollyanna's bedside. "Hello," she said cheerfully. "I'm Miss Hunt, and I'm here to help take care of you."
Pollyanna looked around. "But I don't want to be taken care of! I want to go to school tomorrow!"
Aunt Polly gave a stifled cry.
"Maybe not tomorrow," the nurse said brightly, handing Pollyanna some medicine. "Let's see if these pills help you."
"All right." Pollyanna swallowed the medicine. "But I have to go the day after tomorrow to take exams." She talked for a few more minutes before falling asleep.
For the next week, Pollyanna slept for most of the time. When Pollyanna was finally more alert, Aunt Polly explained the accident again.
"So I'm hurt, not sick," Pollyanna said when she finally understood. "Well, I'm glad of that."
"You're glad?" asked Aunt Polly, sitting by the bed.
"Yes, I'd much rather have broken legs than be a lifelong invalid like Mrs. Snow. Broken legs heal, but lifelong invalids don't get better."

Aunt Polly, who had never mentioned broken legs, suddenly stood up. Walking over to Pollyanna's dressing table, she picked up a hairbrush and put it down. She did that with one thing after another for no apparent reason.

Pollyanna watched a rainbow dancing on her ceiling. It came from the prisms hanging in a window. "I'm glad I don't have smallpox or measles," she said. "The doctor wouldn't let you in my room because those are contagious. And I'm glad I don't have appendicitis—that's painful!"
"You seem to be glad about many things." Aunt Polly's eyes were filled with sorrow as she lovingly gazed at her niece.
"Oh, I am! Lying here gives me lots of time to think about them and to admire my rainbows. I'm so glad Mr. Pendleton gave me those prisms! But most of all I'm glad I was hurt."
"What a thing to say, dear!" Aunt Polly exclaimed.

"But it's true." The little girl laughed softly. "Since I've been hurt, you've called me 'dear' many times. You never did that before. Some of the Ladies' Aiders used to do that, but it's not the same. Oh, Aunt Polly, I'm so glad you belong to me!"
Just then the nurse appeared with some medicine. Aunt Polly, her eyes now filled with tears, fled the room.
That afternoon Nancy ran outside, urgently looking for Tom. The old man was in the barn cleaning harnesses.
"You'll never guess who's sitting in the parlor," Nancy said breathlessly. "John Pendleton, and he's come to see Miss Polly!"
Tom looked up from polishing a brass buckle. "You're joking."
Nancy shook her head. "I let him in myself. And I've been meaning to tell you something: he was never Miss Polly's fiancé."
"I know that."
"Well, that story you told me made me think he was. Anyway, I found out Mr. Pendleton had been in love with Pollyanna's mother, Jennie, not Miss Polly."
"That's right. He was the rich, older man Jennie's parents wanted her to marry."

Nancy picked up a piece of straw, twirling it between two fingers. "I know Miss Polly didn't like Pollyanna's father because he took Jennie far away. But I still don't understand why Miss Polly and Mr. Pendleton dislike each other."

"That goes back to a few years after Jennie got married." Tom handed Nancy the clean harness, and she hung it on the barn wall. "Miss Polly, who was 18 at the time, felt sorry for Mr. Pendleton. She made an effort to be extra nice to him." Tom paused. "Maybe she was too nice because some folks said she was chasing after him."
"Knowing Miss Polly, I'd guess she was embarrassed by all that silly gossip."

"Indeed she was. And this was around the time she broke off her own engagement, so folks were already talking about her. Mr. Pendleton wasn't too keen on the gossip either. After that, she shut herself up in this house, and he shut himself up in his house on Pendleton Hill." Tom started cleaning the leather of another harness with a wet rag. "So where's Miss Polly now?"
"She was just coming downstairs when I ran out here."
Mr. Pendleton attempted to rise from his chair as Aunt Polly entered the sitting room. Without shaking his hand, she took a seat.
"I came to inquire about Pollyanna," Mr. Pendleton said.
"Thank you, she's about the same," Aunt Polly replied sharply.
"But how is she?" Mr. Pendleton pleaded for information.
A quick spasm of pain crossed Aunt Polly's face. "I don't really have much information about her condition."
"But surely the doctor—"
"Dr. Warren himself seems baffled by this case. He's written to a specialist in New York, and that doctor has agreed to come here to examine Pollyanna."
"Can you tell me anything about her injuries?"
"A slight cut on the head, a few bruises, and damage to the spine that caused paralysis from the hips down."
Mr. Pendleton moaned and was silent for a few moments. "How has Pollyanna reacted to being paralyzed?"

"She doesn't seem to really understand, and I hesitate to say more to her until the specialist arrives. She's glad her legs are broken like your leg was. She doesn't want to be a lifelong invalid like Mrs. Snow."
Through a blur of tears, Mr. Pendleton saw the pain in Aunt Polly's own eyes. He remembered how Pollyanna had said she couldn't leave Aunt Polly. And this made him decide to confess something to her.
"I recently tried to get Pollyanna to come live with me," he said. "I thought I would adopt her and make her my heir."

At this point Aunt Polly stopped listening. She thought about what a brilliant future Pollyanna would have with Mr. Pendleton. He had so much more money than she did. Then Aunt Polly remembered Pollyanna's saying that she loved being called "dear" by someone who belonged to her. And Aunt Polly thought about how dreary her own future would be without Pollyanna in the house.
"How did Pollyanna respond to that?" Aunt Polly said harshly.
"She said she wanted to stay with you." Mr. Pendleton pulled himself to his feet. "And she thought you wanted her to stay."
Without looking at Aunt Polly, he headed for the front door. But he heard Aunt Polly by his side.

"When the specialist comes and I know something definite, you'll hear from me." Aunt Polly slipped her trembling hand into Mr. Pendleton's. "Good-bye and thank you for coming. Pollyanna will be pleased to know you were here."
The next day Aunt Polly told Pollyanna that a new doctor had been summoned.
"Another doctor—besides Dr. Warren—might know of a treatment to help you get well faster."

Pollyanna's face lit up with joy. "Dr. Chilton! Oh, Aunt Polly, I've wanted him to visit ever since my accident. But I was afraid you wouldn't allow that because he saw you with the rose in your hair."

Aunt Polly's face turned white, then red, then back to white again. She struggled to keep her voice cheerful. "Oh, no, dear! I didn't mean Dr. Chilton. This new doctor, Dr. Mead, is a very famous one from New York. He knows a great deal about injuries like yours."
Pollyanna's face fell. "I can't believe he knows half as much as Dr. Chilton. After all, Dr. Chilton treated Mr. Pendleton's broken leg. If you don't mind, I'd prefer to have Dr. Chilton."

"But I do mind." Aunt Polly straightened Pollyanna's covers. "I'd do almost anything for you, dear. However, for reasons I can't discuss, I don't want Dr. Chilton here. Besides, he can't know as much as this doctor, who's a specialist."
Pollyanna was not ready to give up. "But, Aunt Polly, if you loved Dr. Chilton—"
"What did you say?" Aunt Polly looked startled.

"If you loved Dr. Chilton instead of that New York doctor, you'd get better faster. I mean, if you were the patient, which you're not." Pollyanna sighed. "I'm just trying to say that I love Dr. Chilton, so he'd make me feel better faster if he came."

Aunt Polly looked relieved when the nurse entered the room. "I'm sorry, Pollyanna," Aunt Polly said. "You must let me decide what's best for you this time. Besides, it's already arranged that the doctor will arrive tomorrow."
As it happened, Dr. Mead did not arrive the next day. Aunt Polly received a telegram that he had suddenly taken ill. This led Pollyanna to plead again for Dr. Chilton.
"It would be so easy for Dr. Chilton to come now," Pollyanna pointed out.
Aunt Polly shook her head. "I'll give you anything you want but that, dear."
As the days passed, Aunt Polly did everything she could to please Pollyanna—except summon Dr. Chilton.

"I wouldn't have believed it, if I didn't see it with my own eyes," Nancy said to Tom. It was early one morning, and they were having breakfast in the kitchen. "Miss Polly didn't used to allow the dog and cat upstairs. Now she lets Buffy and Fluffy tumble on the bed just because it makes Pollyanna happy."
Tom chuckled as he sipped his coffee.

Nancy went on. "When Miss Polly isn't sitting with Pollyanna, she's moving those prisms around to catch the sunlight. She sends for fresh flowers from a neighbor's greenhouse, and here's the most astonishing thing. The other day I caught the nurse fixing Miss Polly's hair while Pollyanna gave instructions. And Miss Polly has worn her hair that way every day just to please that child! She's actually almost—"
"Pretty?" Tom finished her sentence. "I told you she used to be pretty. And I bet she doesn't look so old now."
"That's right." Nancy went to the stove and brought Tom another pancake. "I still haven't figured out who Miss Polly was engaged to."
"And you won't learn that from me!" Tom poured maple syrup on his pancake. "How is Pollyanna these days?"
Nancy sighed. "There's no change. She just lies in bed and tries to be glad about something."
Tom nodded. "From what I hear around town, Pollyanna has told everybody about that Glad Game her father invented."

"Everybody but Miss Polly, who didn't want to hear anything about him. Pollyanna is always telling me how glad she'll be when she can go to school again. Or visit Mrs. Snow or Mr. Pendleton. Or ride in Dr. Chilton's carriage."

Nancy stopped talking and studied her empty plate. When she looked up, her eyes were filled with tears. "Oh, Tom! Pollyanna doesn't realize how far in the future all this gladness is. And both Pollyanna and Miss Polly are getting so thin!"
Tom drank one last swallow of coffee. "The sooner that New York doctor gets here, the better!"
When Dr. Mead finally arrived from New York, Dr. Warren drove him to the Harrington house. Aunt Polly introduced the specialist to Pollyanna and Miss Hunt, the nurse.
"I like you, Dr. Mead!" Pollyanna said after he examined her. "Maybe it's because you look a lot like my doctor."

" Your doctor?" Dr. Mead looked at Dr. Warren, who was talking to the nurse. Dr. Warren was a small man with a brown beard. Dr. Mead was a tall man with a cheerful smile. "But we don't look anything alike!"
Pollyanna glanced at Dr. Warren. "Oh, he isn't my doctor. Dr. Warren is Aunt Polly's doctor. My doctor is Dr. Chilton."
At the mention of Dr. Chilton, Aunt Polly turned red.

"You see, I wanted Dr. Chilton right from the beginning," Pollyanna went on. "But Aunt Polly wanted you. She said you knew more than Dr. Chilton did about broken legs like mine. Of course, if you do, then I'll be glad about that. So, do you?"
"Only time will tell, young lady," Dr. Mead said gently. His smile had disappeared, and he looked quite serious. "Now, if everyone else could join me in the hall, I'd like to speak to you."

What happened next upset everyone in the house. As the adults talked in the hall, Fluffy, the cat, poked at Pollyanna's door. If the door had been closed, she would not have succeeded. But Fluffy managed to use her nose and paw to push the door until it stood ajar. The cat jumped onto the bed, just as Aunt Polly gave an anguished cry.
"Not that! Oh, Dr. Mead, anything but that. You don't mean . . ." Aunt Polly had to force herself to say the awful words. "You don't mean she'll never walk again !"
From the bedroom Pollyanna cried out in terror. "Aunt Polly! Aunt Polly!"
Seeing the open door and realizing Pollyanna had overheard, Aunt Polly gave a low moan. Then, for the first time in her life, she fainted. Fortunately, Dr. Mead caught her before she hit the floor.
"I'm coming, Pollyanna!" Miss Hunt stumbled toward the open door while the two doctors tended to Aunt Polly.
In Pollyanna's room Fluffy was vainly trying to attract the panicked child's attention.
"Miss Hunt, please, I want Aunt Polly." Pollyanna's eyes were wide with fear. "I want her right now. Quick, please get her for me!"
The nurse closed the door and hurried over to the bed.
"She can't come just this minute, dear. She will come a little later. What do you want? Is there something I can get for you?"
Pollyanna shook her head. "I want to know more about what she just said. Did you hear her? I want Aunt Polly. She said something, and I need her to tell me it isn't true."
Miss Hunt tried to speak but couldn't find the right words. Something in the nurse's face added to Pollyanna's terror.
"Miss Hunt, you did hear her! It is true! You mean, I'll never walk again?"
"There, there, dear, don't—" The nurse choked back her own tears. "Maybe Dr. Mead didn't know what he was saying. Perhaps he was mistaken. Lots of things could happen."
"But Aunt Polly said he knew more than anybody else about broken legs like mine!"
"Yes, I know, but all doctors make mistakes sometimes. Don't think anything more about it right now."

Pollyanna flung out her arms. "But I can't help thinking about it," she sobbed. "It's all I can think about. How will I go to school or visit my friends? If I can't walk, how will I ever be glad about anything ?"
While Pollyanna sobbed, Miss Hunt had been preparing some medicine. "Just take this, dear," she said. "Maybe after you rest, things will seem brighter."

Pollyanna took the medicine and sipped the water offered by Miss Hunt. "That sounds like something Father used to say. But he'd never been told he wouldn't walk again. Nothing could be worse than that, could it?"
Miss Hunt had no answer for Pollyanna's question.

Aunt Polly sent Nancy to deliver the bad news to Mr. Pendleton. Normally Nancy would have been excited to see inside his mysterious mansion. But now she was too upset to even glance around the library, where she waited for Mr. Pendleton.
"Well?" he said upon entering the room.
"Sir, the New York doctor says Pollyanna will never walk again!"
Mr. Pendleton sank into the nearest chair. "Poor little girl." He covered his eyes with his hand and moaned. "My little prism girl! She'll never dance in the sunshine again."
Nancy could not believe that John Pendleton—a grumpy miser—was showing such emotion.
He looked up. "I hope Pollyanna doesn't know this horrible news."
"That's the worst part, sir. She does." Nancy sobbed. "And she can't think of anything to be glad about."
"I know how much she loves to play her Glad Game."
"I tried to cheer her up by reminding her what she told Mrs. Snow. But she said it's one thing to tell a lifelong invalid how to play the game. And quite another when you're the lifelong invalid."

Mr. Pendleton offered Nancy his handkerchief, and she wiped her eyes before continuing. "Thank you, sir. Pollyanna used to say the game was more interesting when it was hard. But now she keeps dwelling on the fact that she'll never walk again. I must leave, sir, because Miss Polly needs me at home."

Nancy hopped up but turned at the door. "Pollyanna feels bad that she can't bring Jimmy Bean to visit you. She fears he didn't make a good impression the first time." She hesitated. "I'm sure she'd be glad to hear that you were going to visit him."
Mr. Pendleton shook his head. "I'm sorry, but I have no plans to see him."

The entire town soon knew that Pollyanna would never walk again. Many people recognized Pollyanna as the cheerful girl who always greeted them with a smile. And almost everyone was familiar with the Glad Game. Aunt Polly was surprised by the number of visitors—friends and strangers—who arrived at her door. Many people were in tears as they handed Aunt Polly flowers or other gifts for Pollyanna.
When John Pendleton arrived one day, he had an important message for Pollyanna. "Please tell her that I've seen Jimmy Bean. She'll be glad to know that I'm thinking of adopting him."
Aunt Polly was so shocked that she couldn't control her reaction. "Jimmy Bean?" she gasped. "You're going to adopt that . . . that boy?"
"Yes, and I think Pollyanna will understand why."
After Mr. Pendleton left, Aunt Polly went upstairs and delivered his message. "Mr. Pendleton said you'd be glad about this news."

Pollyanna broke into a wide grin. "Glad? Of course I'm glad! Oh, Aunt Polly, I've wanted to find a place for Jimmy to live. And Mr. Pendleton's house is such a lovely place. Besides, I'm glad for Mr. Pendleton because he'll have a child's presence."
"A what?"
"Mr. Pendleton thinks it takes a spouse's hand and heart or a child's presence to make a house a home. Dr. Chilton thinks that too."
Aunt Polly looked startled. " Dr. Chilton ! How do you know what he thinks?"
"He told me himself. He says the rooms where he lives aren't really a home."
While Aunt Polly stared silently out the window, Pollyanna went on. "So I asked him why he didn't get a spouse's hand and heart."
"Pollyanna!" Aunt Polly turned abruptly and shook her finger at Pollyanna. "Why did you do that?"
"Because he seemed so sad."
There was another question that Aunt Polly wanted to ask. She hesitated, almost afraid to hear the answer. She sat down and gathered her courage before asking, "What did he say?"
"He said you can't always get a spouse just by asking. I know he wants a wife because I heard him say so, even though he spoke very quietly."
"What did he say?" Aunt Polly asked again in her own soft voice.
"He said he'd do almost anything to have one particular woman's hand and heart."
Aunt Polly stood up hurriedly and went back to the window.
"What's the matter, Aunt Polly?"
"Er . . . nothing, dear. It's time to move this pendant so it catches more light."
One afternoon Milly Snow visited Aunt Polly. "I came to find out how Pollyanna is doing," Milly said.
Aunt Polly pushed back a loose strand of hair. "About the same, and how is your mother?"
"That's what I want you to tell Pollyanna. Mother is so much better, and it's all thanks to Pollyanna and her game."

Aunt Polly wanted to ask about the game, but Milly kept on talking. "Mother just used to sit in her dark room and complain. But now she keeps the curtains open and takes an interest in her appearance."
"That's nice."

"After Pollyanna told Mother she should be glad she has arms and hands, Mother wanted to do something useful. So she knits blankets for charity, and her room is full of brightly colored yarn. I used to hate to go in there, but now I'm glad to. Anyway . . ." Milly took a deep breath. "We thought if Pollyanna knew she'd changed our lives, she might be glad." Milly stood up to go. "So will you tell her?"
"Of course," Aunt Polly said, though she wasn't quite sure what Milly had been talking about.
Many other visitors left mysterious messages for Pollyanna. When Widow Benton arrived, she was dressed in black as usual. But she was also wearing a blue ribbon around her neck.
"Please tell Pollyanna about my ribbon," Widow Benton said to Aunt Polly. "I hope she'll be glad I've taken her suggestion to wear some color."

That same day a stranger named Mrs. Tarbell arrived. She, too, was dressed in black, as if in mourning. "I've been staying at the hotel in town and taking long walks every day for my health. I always enjoyed walking with Pollyanna. She reminded me of my daughter who died years ago. Could you just tell her that I'm glad now? I'd rather not explain why."
After Mrs. Tarbell left, Aunt Polly hurried upstairs. "Pollyanna, do you know a Mrs. Tarbell?"
"Oh, yes. She's awfully sick and sad. We go for long walks together. I mean, we used to . . ." Pollyanna's voice broke, and two big tears rolled down her cheeks.
Aunt Polly cleared her throat. "She said to tell you she's glad now."
Pollyanna clapped her hands and almost smiled. "Oh, I'm so glad!"
"She said something about a game. What was she talking about?"
"Nothing." Pollyanna turned her head away. "I can't talk about it."
Pollyanna seemed so upset that Aunt Polly left her alone. She went downstairs to the kitchen, where Nancy was ironing.

"Nancy! All of Pollyanna's visitors want me to tell her they're playing some game. Half the town is wearing bright colors or doing new things all because of Pollyanna. I tried to ask her about it, but she wouldn't tell me." Aunt Polly stamped her foot. "What is this absurd game everyone's playing?"
To Aunt Polly's surprise and dismay, Nancy burst into tears. When Nancy had calmed down, she told the story of the doll and the crutches in the donation box.
"She was glad for crutches?" Aunt Polly choked back a sob. "But why wouldn't she tell me about the Glad Game?"

Nancy picked up the napkin she'd just ironed and wrung it like a wet rag. "Begging your pardon, ma'am, but you wouldn't let her. You told her not to speak of her father, and it was his game. Pollyanna desperately wanted to play it, so she told a few people, and the game spread throughout the town. She was always so cheerful . . ." Nancy tried to smooth the wrinkled napkin. "Now everyone is sad she isn't glad anymore."
"Well, I know someone who'll play that game with her right now!"
Aunt Polly hurried back upstairs to Pollyanna's room. When she told Pollyanna that Nancy had explained the game to her, Pollyanna's face lit up with joy.
"Oh, Aunt Polly, you're the person I've most wanted to play the Glad Game with!" Pollyanna held out her arms, and Aunt Polly hugged her.
"Do you have any idea what you've accomplished?" Aunt Polly smiled broadly. "The whole town is happier because you taught everyone the Glad Game."
Pollyanna suddenly looked serious. "I'm so glad I had legs that worked. Because without them, I couldn't have done that!"

One by one the short winter days came and went. But for Pollyanna the days were long and sometimes full of pain. While other children went skating on the frozen ice or sledding on the snowy hills, Pollyanna lay in bed.
Now that Aunt Polly was playing the Glad Game, Pollyanna tried to be cheerful. Like Mrs. Snow, Pollyanna had taken up knitting. "At least I can still use my arms and hands!" she said to Aunt Polly.
"Hold out your arms, and we'll wind this yarn into a ball," Aunt Polly said.
They had just finished when Nancy entered the room. "You have two visitors, Pollyanna," she said.
"Two at once?" Pollyanna was delighted. "I rarely have one."
"I'd better go see who they are," Aunt Polly said.
A few minutes later, Mr. Pendleton and Jimmy entered Pollyanna's room. Mr. Pendleton was carrying another prism, and Jimmy had a box of chocolates.
"We won't stay long," Mr. Pendleton said. "I just wanted you to know how well Jimmy's doing. He's turning into a fine boy!"
"I have a wonderful home now," Jimmy added. "Mr. Pendleton is turning into a fine family!"
"I owe it all to you!" Jimmy and Mr. Pendleton said to Pollyanna at the same time. They looked at each other and laughed.
Noticing how happy they were together, Pollyanna smiled. "I'm so glad!"

As spring arrived, there was little change in Pollyanna's condition. The townspeople kept up with the latest news, but everyone felt discouraged. Despite Dr. Mead's treatments, Pollyanna was not improving.

Dr. Chilton was especially concerned about her. Although he never spoke to Aunt Polly, he always managed to hear about Pollyanna's condition. "I need to do more than worry about Pollyanna," he thought one day in his office.
The next Saturday morning, he went to see Mr. Pendleton. It was a lovely spring day, and the windows were open as the two men sat in the library.

"I've come to you because you've lived in this town your whole life," Dr. Chilton said. "Of anyone here, you know the most about my past relationship with Polly Harrington. I want to examine Pollyanna. I must examine her!"
"Why can't you?"

"You know very well that I haven't been inside that house for over 15 years. When Miss Polly and I quarreled, she said she'd never ask me there again. Not unless she was ready to beg my forgiveness and marry me."
Mr. Pendleton thought for a moment. "I don't understand why you have to be asked to the house. Can't you go on your own?"
Dr. Chilton shook his head. "Out of courtesy to Dr. Warren and Dr. Mead, I can't just barge in."
"Maybe you need to focus on making up with Miss Polly. What did you quarrel about?"

"Forget the quarrel." The doctor made an impatient gesture and stood up. "It was a silly argument about nothing. What's important is that if I can see Pollyanna, there's a 90 percent chance she'll walk again." As Dr. Chilton said that in a loud voice, he paced over to the window.
In the garden below, Jimmy was pulling weeds. He stopped weeding and sat up, his ears wide open.
"Pollyanna! Walk again!" Mr. Pendleton exclaimed. "What are you talking about?"
"I have a doctor friend who specializes in this type of paralysis. From what I've been able to gather, Pollyanna's case sounds similar to one he just cured."
"You must see her right away!" Mr. Pendleton was now standing too. "Couldn't you see her through Dr. Warren?"
"No!" Dr. Chilton slammed his fist on Mr. Pendleton's desk. "Dr. Warren suggested early on that I examine Pollyanna. But Miss Polly said no so firmly that Dr. Warren didn't dare mention it again."
"Miss Polly must be made to ask you!"
"But how? She's too proud and angry to ask me herself."
"Miss Polly must be made to understand how vitally important this is," Mr. Pendleton said.
"And who's going to do that?" Dr. Chilton said bitterly.
Mr. Pendleton groaned. "I have no idea."
Outside the window Jimmy had hardly moved since he started eavesdropping. "I know," he whispered. " I'm going to do it!"
As fast as he could, Jimmy ran down Pendleton Hill toward Miss Polly's house.
By the time Jimmy Bean reached Aunt Polly's house, he was out of breath. He was also still clutching a gardening tool.

"I can't bring this inside!" he thought, hiding the tool behind a bush in Aunt Polly's garden. Then he boldly knocked on the front door. "I need to see Miss Polly right away," he said to Nancy when she opened the door. "It's urgent."
Nancy found Aunt Polly in her room, writing a letter. "Jimmy Bean is here, and he wants to talk to you, ma'am. He says it's important."
"Me?" Aunt Polly was clearly surprised. "Are you sure he didn't mean Miss Pollyanna? He may see her for a few minutes, if he likes."
"Yes, ma'am, but he insists you're the one he needs to talk to."
"Very well, I'll come downstairs." Aunt Polly put the letter in an envelope and rose from her chair.

In the sitting room, she found Jimmy, who started speaking at once. "Ma'am, I suppose you'll think what I'm saying is dreadful. But I'm doing it for Pollyanna, so I hope you won't be offended. I'd do anything for Pollyanna—and you would too, if you thought there was a chance she could walk again. I guess it's pride that's keeping you from asking Dr. Chilton to come."
"What?" Aunt Polly's look of confusion quickly changed to outrage.
Jimmy sighed. "I don't mean to make you angry. That's why I thought I'd begin by telling you about Pollyanna's walking again. I thought you'd listen to that."
"Jimmy, what are you talking about? Start your story at the beginning, and be sure I understand everything before you continue."
"All right." Jimmy wet his lips and started again. "First Dr. Chilton came to see Mr. Pendleton, and they talked in the library. Do you understand that?"
"Yes, Jimmy." Aunt Polly's voice was rather faint. "Go on."
"Well, the window was open, and I was weeding the flowerbed underneath. So it was easy for me to hear what they were saying about—"
"You mean you were eavesdropping? Oh, Jimmy, you should never sneak around, trying to overhear conversations!"

Jimmy put his hands on his hips and stuck his chin out defiantly. "I wasn't sneaking around, and I'm glad I listened. And you will be too, when I tell you what I heard. They were talking about Pollyanna walking again!"
"What do you mean?" Aunt Polly leaned forward, eager to hear the rest of Jimmy's story.
"Dr. Chilton knows some doctor somewhere that he thinks can cure Pollyanna. Dr. Chilton needs to see her first, to be sure. But he told Mr. Pendleton you wouldn't let him in the house."
"Oh, Jimmy, I couldn't . . . I can't!" Aunt Polly was wringing her hands helplessly. "I mean, I don't know—"

"Exactly!" Jimmy said with a look of triumph. "That's why I'm here, so you will know what's going on. I'm not sure I have this right, but . . . Dr. Chilton said he'd offend Dr. Warren if he came here without your permission. And he wished somebody could make you understand how important this is. But neither Dr. Chilton nor Mr. Pendleton knew anybody who could do that. That's why I decided to do it." Jimmy took a deep breath. "So, have I made you understand?"
"Yes, Jimmy, but who is this doctor? Is Dr. Chilton sure this man could make Pollyanna walk?"

"All I know is he cured someone just like Pollyanna. Anyway, Dr. Chilton didn't seem worried about the doctor. You're the real problem. I mean, now do you understand why Dr. Chilton has to see Pollyanna?"
Aunt Polly was breathing heavily, and Jimmy thought she was about to cry. "Yes, Jimmy, you've done an excellent job. Dr. Warren is upstairs now with Pollyanna, and I need to speak to him right away!"
A minute later Dr. Warren was surprised to meet a flustered Aunt Polly in the hall. He was even more surprised by what she said.

"Dr. Warren, you once asked me to allow Dr. Chilton to examine Pollyanna, and I refused." Miss Polly looked the doctor right in the eye. "Some new information has made me reconsider that decision. Please ask him to come as soon as possible!"
The next time Dr. Warren visited Pollyanna, he was accompanied by another doctor.
"Dr. Chilton! I'm so glad to see you!" Pollyanna shouted happily before she remembered her aunt's opinion of him. "Oh, but if Aunt Polly doesn't want you—"
"It's all right, my dear." Aunt Polly put down the book she'd been reading to Pollyanna. "I told Dr. Warren that I wanted Dr. Chilton to examine you."
"Oh, you asked him to come." Pollyanna smiled contentedly at this explanation.
"Yes, dear, I asked him. That is . . ." Seeing the adoring look on Dr. Chilton's face, Aunt Polly turned red, sprang from her chair, and ran from the room.

Dr. Chilton followed Aunt Polly with his eyes. "Well, Pollyanna . . ." He cleared his throat, but his voice was still shaking with emotion. "Well, Pollyanna, you've just done the gladdest thing of all!"
"I have?" Pollyanna didn't understand what was going on.
"Yes, you've done something to make me very glad. Now let's take a look at those legs."
At the end of the day, Aunt Polly returned to Pollyanna's bedside.
"Oh, Aunt Polly, you look so pretty!" Pollyanna said. "You look like you did when I dressed you up with the rose and shawl. What has happened?"

Aunt Polly laughed, a joyous laugh that Pollyanna had never heard before. "I want you to be the first person to know—Dr. Chilton is going to be your uncle Thomas! We're getting married! We're both so happy, and it's all thanks to you."
"Oh, Aunt Polly, that's wonderful news!" Pollyanna started to clap her hands but stopped. "Wait a minute. Does that mean you were the woman whose hand and heart he wanted a long time ago?"
Aunt Polly nodded. "We broke off our engagement after a silly argument, but you brought us together again."
Pollyanna suddenly understood. "So that's why Dr. Chilton said I'd done the gladdest thing of all. I'm so glad right now that I don't even mind about my legs!"

"Someday you might . . ." Aunt Polly didn't dare to raise Pollyanna's hopes that she might walk again. She smoothed Pollyanna's hair with her hand. "Next week you're going on a long trip to stay with a great doctor. He's a friend of Dr. Chilton's, and he runs a clinic just for patients like you. We're going to see if there's anything he can do for you."
"Oh, Aunt Polly, if he's a friend of Dr. Chilton's, I'm sure he can help me."
Many months later Aunt Polly and Uncle Thomas received a letter that made them very glad.
Dear Aunt Polly and Uncle Thomas,
I can walk! Today I walked all the way from my bed to the window! It was only six steps, but oh, how good it felt to walk again.

All the doctors stood around and smiled. A lady who walked for the first time last week stood at my door and watched. Another lady, who hopes to walk next month, lay on the other bed in my room and clapped her hands. It was like a party except both ladies and all the nurses were crying. I don't understand why everybody was in tears. I wanted to sing and shout and bang doors!

After walking today, I don't mind that I've been here almost ten months. You made sure that I didn't miss the most important event that happened during that time: your wedding! I still can't believe you got married right here at my bedside! Not only did I get to attend your wedding, but so did all the doctors and nurses and patients and staff. Your wedding made everybody at the clinic feel glad!

The doctors say I'll soon be going home. I wish I could walk all the way there. I don't think I'll ever want to ride anywhere again. (Well, maybe I'll want an occasional ride in your carriage, Uncle Thomas. I always loved that!)

Oh, I'm so glad about everything these days. I'm even glad that I lost the use of my legs for a while. You never realize how lovely legs are until you don't have them. (I mean, legs that work, of course!) I'm going to walk eight steps tomorrow!
With lots of love to everyone in Beldingsville,
Pollyanna
